Here are some fun, hands-on circuit projects you can build at home. They range from super-simple paper circuits to more advanced microcontroller designs—pick one based on your experience and the parts you have on hand:

• LED Mood Lamp with 555 Timer  
  – Use a 555 timer IC to make an LED fade in and out. Adjust resistors or a potentiometer for different blink rates.

• Paper Circuits Greeting Cards  
  – Draw a circuit on cardstock using copper tape, a coin cell battery, and surface-mount LEDs. Great for beginners and art-meets-electronics!

• Clap-Activated Switch  
  – Build a simple sound detector (microphone + amplifier) that toggles an LED or small motor each time you clap.

• Light-Sensitive Night Light  
  – Use a photoresistor (LDR) and a transistor to automatically turn on an LED when the room gets dark.

• Electronic Dice (7-Segment Display)  
  – Wire up a handful of NAND gates or use a small microcontroller to produce random numbers on a single 7-segment LED.

• Touch-Sensitive Lamp  
  – Make a capacitive touch sensor (using foil or a metal plate) that toggles an LED strip without any mechanical switch.

• Theremin-Style Theremin  
  – Build a simple oscillator whose pitch varies with the distance of your hand from an antenna—use a 555 timer or two LC circuits.

• DIY FM Radio Receiver  
  – Assemble a cheap FM radio kit or build a basic superheterodyne receiver on a solderless breadboard.

• Arduino-Powered Plant Watering System  
  – Hook up soil-moisture probes, a small pump or valve, and let an Arduino automatically water your plants when they get too dry.

• Solar-Powered USB Charger  
  – Combine a small solar panel, charge-controller circuit, and a 5 V boost converter to charge phones or power USB gadgets.

• PWM Fan Speed Controller  
  – Learn about pulse-width modulation by building a circuit that lets you dial a computer fan’s speed up or down.

• IR Remote-Controlled LED Strip  
  – Use an IR receiver module, a microcontroller (or discrete logic), and MOSFETs to switch on/off or dim an LED strip with any TV remote.

• Electronic Piano/Keyboard  
  – Wire up a row of pushbuttons each connected to a square-wave generator or microcontroller pin, and play simple tunes on a small speaker.

• Breadboard Logic Puzzle Kit  
  – Set up a series of gates (AND, OR, XOR) and challenge yourself or friends to rewire them to achieve different Boolean outputs.

Each project can be scaled up or down in complexity—swap discrete components for integrated modules, add enclosures, or integrate sensors and displays to customize your build. Have fun exploring the world of circuits!

To evaluate if the Transformer can generalize to other tasks we performed experiments on English constituency parsing. This task presents specific challenges: the output is subject to strong structural constraints and is significantly longer than the input. Furthermore, RNN sequence-to-sequence models have not been able to attain state-of-the-art results in small-data regimes.
Question: What is English constituency parsing?
instruction: Answer the question about the paper after reading it carefully.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text an answer relevant to the question in the given input?
Is the answer in the generated text correct according to the paper in the given input?
output:
English constituency parsing is the task of taking an English sentence as input and producing a labeled, hierarchical “bracketed” tree that reveals its phrase‐structure (constituents).  Concretely, a parser must

• break the sentence into subphrases (e.g. noun phrases NP, verb phrases VP, etc.)  
• nest those subphrases into a full syntactic tree (e.g. an S node for the whole sentence)  
• assign each node a grammatical category  

For example, the sentence  
  “The cat sat on the mat”  
might be parsed as  
  (S  
    (NP The cat)  
    (VP sat (PP on (NP the mat))))  

Constituency parsing thus produces a tree structure subject to the strong structural constraints of English grammar.

Problem Title: Painting the Fence with Exactly K Color–Blocks

Problem Statement:  
You have a fence consisting of N contiguous segments, numbered 1 through N. You want to paint each segment in one of M available colors (colors are labeled 1 through M). Painting segment i with color j costs cost[i][j]. A “color–block” is defined as a maximal contiguous run of fence segments painted the same color.  

Your goal is to paint all N segments so that the total number of color–blocks is exactly K, and the total painting cost is minimized. If it is impossible to achieve exactly K blocks, output –1.

Input Format:  
• Line 1: Three integers N, M, and K  
• Next N lines: line i+1 contains M space–separated integers cost[i][1], cost[i][2], …, cost[i][M]  

Output Format:  
• A single integer: the minimum total cost to paint all N segments with exactly K color–blocks, or –1 if it cannot be done.

Constraints:  
• 1 ≤ N ≤ 200  
• 1 ≤ M ≤ 50  
• 1 ≤ K ≤ N  
• 0 ≤ cost[i][j] ≤ 10^6  

Example 1:  
Input:  
3 2 3  
1 10  
10 1  
1 1  

Explanation:  
We need exactly 3 blocks on 3 segments, so every adjacent pair must change color.  
One optimal painting is [1, 2, 1] with cost = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.  
Output:  
3

Example 2:  
Input:  
4 3 2  
5 3 4  
2 1 3  
3 2 4  
4 3 2  

Explanation:  
We want exactly 2 blocks on segments 1–4.  
One optimal solution: paint segments [2, 2, 3, 3].  
  – Block 1 is color 2 on segments 1–2: cost = 3 + 1 = 4  
  – Block 2 is color 3 on segments 3–4: cost = 4 + 2 = 6  
Total cost = 4 + 6 = 10.  
Output:  
10

Example 3:  
Input:  
5 2 1  
1 2  
2 1  
3 3  
1 2  
2 1  

Explanation:  
We want exactly 1 block (all segments same color).  
  – If all are color 1: cost = 1+2+3+1+2 = 9  
  – If all are color 2: cost = 2+1+3+2+1 = 9  
Minimum = 9.  
Output:  
9

Hint / Solution Sketch:  
Define dp[i][j][b] = minimum cost to paint segments 1..i so that segment i has color j and there are exactly b blocks in total.  
Transition:  
For each i from 1 to N, for each color j (1..M), and for each previous color p (1..M):  
  if j == p:
    dp[i][j][b] = min(dp[i][j][b], dp[i–1][p][b] + cost[i][j])  
  else:
    dp[i][j][b] = min(dp[i][j][b], dp[i–1][p][b–1] + cost[i][j])  

Initialize dp[1][j][1] = cost[1][j] for all j; other entries = ∞.  
Answer = min over j of dp[N][j][K], or –1 if it remains ∞.  
Time complexity: O(N × M × M × K) which is acceptable for N≤200, M≤50, K≤N.

Trusty Jeans  
No fall getaway is truly set until you’ve packed a reliable pair of jeans. Denim is the ultimate wardrobe workhorse—durable enough for rugged weekend hikes, polished enough for dinner reservations, and endlessly versatile for layering when the temperature drops. Best of all? Jeans can be worn all year and look good with everything, making them an unbeatable travel essential.  

Why jeans earn a permanent spot in your suitcase  
• All-season adaptability: From breezy summer mornings to crisp autumn evenings, denim’s medium-weight fabric insulates just enough to keep you comfortable without overheating.  
• Effortless styling: Pair dark-wash jeans with a chunky knit sweater and ankle boots for daytime exploring, then swap into heeled bootcuts and a blazer for a sleek evening look.  
• Mix-and-match champion: Whether your trip features museum-hopping in the city or lakeside strolls in the countryside, jeans serve as the common denominator that ties together graphic tees, flannel shirts, faux-leather jackets, sweaters, and even silk blouses.  

Tips for packing and styling your go-to pair  
1. Choose a flattering cut: A mid-rise straight-leg or a slim bootcut silhouette transitions flawlessly from casual to dressed-up moments.  
2. Optimize your color palette: A classic indigo wash is endlessly versatile; black or deep gray jeans add a modern edge when you want to appear a touch more polished.  
3. Embrace layering: In fall’s unpredictable weather, cuff your jeans over tights or knee-high socks for extra warmth, then throw on an oversized cardigan or a tailored coat.  
4. Accessorize smartly: A colorful scarf or statement belt can refresh your denim look each day without weighing down your luggage.  

No matter where your fall travels take you—leaf-peeping in New England, wine-tasting in California’s vineyards, or cozying up in a mountain lodge—your trusty jeans will be the dependable, stylish companion that never lets you down.

Here’s a sample 9-day, light-to-moderate activity family itinerary—arrive in Casablanca, depart from Marrakech. You’ll balance cultural sightseeing, easy walks, scenic drives, a desert stay and a cooking class.  

Day 1 – Arrival in Casablanca  
• Morning/Afternoon  
  – Arrive at Mohammed V Airport (Casablanca).  
  – Transfer to your centrally located hotel or riad.  
  – Visit the Hassan II Mosque (guided tour, mostly flat walking).  
• Evening  
  – Dinner on the Corniche overlooking the Atlantic.  
  – Overnight in Casablanca.  

Day 2 – Casablanca → Chefchaouen (approx. 4¼ hr drive)  
• Morning  
  – Breakfast at the hotel.  
  – Depart for the Blue City, Chefchaouen, via the Rif foothills.  
• Afternoon  
  – Check into your riad in the medina.  
  – Leisurely stroll through the blue-washed alleys, visit Plaza Uta el-Hamman.  
• Evening  
  – Enjoy a relaxed dinner on a rooftop terrace.  
  – Overnight in Chefchaouen.  

Day 3 – Chefchaouen → Fès (approx. 4 hr drive)  
• Morning  
  – Optional gentle 45-minute walk up to the Spanish Mosque viewpoint for panoramic village views.  
  – Return to riad for late breakfast.  
• Midday  
  – Drive to Fès, stopping en route for lunch.  
• Afternoon/Evening  
  – Check into your Fès riad.  
  – Short evening walk in the medina to get a first glimpse of the tanneries and souks.  
  – Overnight in Fès.  

Day 4 – Guided Fès Medina Tour  
• Morning  
  – Local guide leads you through the UNESCO-listed medina:  
    • Al-Qarawiyyin University & mosque (exterior).  
    • 14th-century tanneries (overlook platform).  
    • Artisan quarters (leather, metalwork, ceramics).  
• Afternoon  
  – Lunch in a traditional courtyard café.  
  – Free time for optional shopping or a gentle horse-drawn carriage (“caleche”) ride.  
• Evening  
  – Return to riad; consider an early-evening hammam & massage (optional, light).  
  – Overnight in Fès.  

Day 5 – Fès → Merzouga Desert (approx. 7 hr drive with stops)  
• Early Morning  
  – Depart Fès after breakfast.  
• En Route  
  – Ifrane (“Little Switzerland”) and cedar forest at Azrou (short stroll, chance to see Barbary macaques).  
  – Ziz Valley viewpoints—photo stops.  
• Late Afternoon/Evening  
  – Arrive Merzouga area; transfer to a desert kasbah-style lodge.  
  – Evening camel ride into the dunes to watch sunset.  
  – Arrive at a Berber desert camp. Traditional dinner under the stars.  
  – Overnight in a desert tent (shared or family private).  

Day 6 – Merzouga → Todra Gorge → Dades Valley (approx. 3½ hr total driving)  
• Dawn  
  – Watch sunrise over the dunes, light breakfast at camp.  
  – Camel trek back to Merzouga.  
• Mid-Morning  
  – Depart for Todra Gorge.  
• Afternoon  
  – Short, easy 1-hour walk along the river at the base of the gorge.  
  – Continue to Dades Valley via scenic “Route of a Thousand Kasbahs.”  
• Evening  
  – Check into a hotel perched over the valley.  
  – Sunset stroll in the valley floor if you wish.  
  – Overnight in Dades.  

Day 7 – Dades Valley → Aït Benhaddou → Marrakech (approx. 6–7 hr driving with stops)  
• Morning  
  – After breakfast, head to Ouarzazate—visit Taourirt Kasbah.  
  – Short drive to Aït Benhaddou (UNESCO ksar). Guided walk through the earthen village.  
• Afternoon  
  – Cross the High Atlas via Tizi n’Tichka Pass (2 226 m). Scenic photo stops.  
  – Arrive in Marrakech late afternoon.  
• Evening  
  – Check into your riad in the medina.  
  – Dinner at Djemaa el-Fna square (street-food stalls if you’re adventurous).  
  – Overnight in Marrakech.  

Day 8 – Marrakech Highlights & Family Cooking Class  
• Morning  
  – Guided half-day tour of Marrakech:  
    • Koutoubia Mosque (exterior).  
    • Bahia Palace and Saadian Tombs (short walks).  
    • Wander the souks—spice square, leather goods, carpets.  
• Lunch & Afternoon  
  – Hands-on Moroccan cooking class: learn to make tagine, salads, mint tea.  
  – Enjoy the feast you’ve prepared.  
• Evening  
  – Free time for rooftop café views, optional evening stroll back to Djemaa el-Fna.  
  – Overnight in Marrakech.  

Day 9 – Jardin Majorelle & Departure  
• Morning  
  – Breakfast at the riad.  
  – Visit Yves Saint Laurent’s Jardin Majorelle and the adjacent Berber Museum (flat, easy walking).  
• Midday  
  – Return to medina for a final lunch or last-minute shopping (optional).  
  – Private transfer to Marrakech Menara Airport for your flight home.  

Notes & Tips  
• Activity level remains light to moderate—mostly cultural walks, easy hikes, scenic drives.  
• Driving days average 4–7 hours; you’ll break them up with interesting stops.  
• Family-friendly pace: late starts some days, free afternoons to rest, choice of optional extensions (hammam, short mule ride in Atlas, extra desert night).  
• Accommodations: mix of riads in the medinas, comfortable desert camp tents, valley-view hotels.  
• Pack layers: desert nights can be cool, mountain passes may be chilly. Comfortable walking shoes and sun protection recommended.

Acceptance Criteria

1. Search Field Presence  
   - A visible, single-line text input (“Search”) is present on the hotel listing page.  
   - The input displays placeholder text such as “Search by city, hotel name or street.”

2. Search Input Behavior  
   - The user can click into the field and type any combination of letters, numbers, spaces or common punctuation.  
   - The field accepts at least 2 characters before performing a search.

3. Triggering Search  
   - Hitting the Enter key within the field initiates the search.  
   - Clicking a “Search” button next to the field (or a magnifying-glass icon) also initiates the search.

4. Matching Logic  
   - The search is case-insensitive.  
   - Partial matches are allowed (e.g. typing “Hil” returns “Hilton Garden Inn”).  
   - The system searches across three data fields: city name, hotel name, and street address.

5. Displaying Results  
   - When one or more hotels match the query, they appear in a list or grid below the search field.  
   - Each result displays at least the hotel name, city, street address, and a thumbnail image.

6. No-results Handling  
   - If no hotels match the query, display a message such as “No hotels found matching ‘XYZ’.”  
   - Provide an option to clear the search field and retry (e.g. a clear-field “×” icon).

7. Performance  
   - Search results load within 2 seconds of triggering the search on average network conditions.

Here’s a step-by-step guide to performing lying leg raises safely and effectively:

1. Setup and Starting Position  
   • Lie flat on your back on an exercise mat or firm surface.  
   • Extend your legs straight and keep your arms by your sides, palms down.  
   • Press your lower back gently into the floor—avoid an excessive arch.  

2. Execution  
   a. Engage your core by drawing your navel toward your spine.  
   b. Keeping your legs straight (or with a slight bend in the knees if needed), lift them together toward the ceiling.  
   c. Raise until your legs form about a 90° angle with your torso, or as high as you can without lifting your lower back off the floor.  
   d. Pause briefly at the top, maintaining tension in your abdominal muscles.  
   e. Slowly lower your legs back down, controlling the movement until your feet are just a few inches from the floor.  

3. Breathing  
   • Inhale as you lower your legs.  
   • Exhale as you lift them.  

4. Repetitions and Sets  
   • Beginners: 2–3 sets of 8–12 reps.  
   • Intermediate/Advanced: 3–4 sets of 12–20 reps or add ankle weights for more resistance.  
   • Rest 30–60 seconds between sets.  

5. Common Form Tips  
   • Keep the lower back pressed into the mat—if your back arches, lift your hips slightly or bend your knees more.  
   • Move in a slow, controlled manner rather than letting gravity do the work.  
   • Focus on using your lower abs to lift and lower the legs.  

6. Common Mistakes to Avoid  
   • Swinging the legs or using momentum.  
   • Letting the lower back arch and lift off the floor.  
   • Lifting the head and neck—keep them relaxed on the mat.  

7. Variations and Progressions  
   • Bent-Knee Leg Raises: Reduce hamstring tension by bending the knees.  
   • Hanging Leg Raises: Hang from a pull-up bar and lift knees or straight legs.  
   • Weighted Leg Raises: Hold a dumbbell or ankle weights for added resistance.  

By following these steps and focusing on controlled movement, you’ll target your lower abdominal muscles safely and effectively.

input: Few-shot learning (FSL) is one of the key future steps in machine learning and raises a lot of attention. In this paper, we focus on the FSL problem of dialogue understanding, which contains two closely related tasks: intent detection and slot filling. Dialogue understanding has been proven to benefit a lot from jointly learning the two sub-tasks. However, such joint learning becomes challenging in the few-shot scenarios: on the one hand, the sparsity of samples greatly magnifies the difficulty of modeling the connection between the two tasks; on the other hand, how to jointly learn multiple tasks in the few-shot setting is still less investigated. In response to this, we introduce FewJoint, the first FSL benchmark for joint dialogue understanding. FewJoint provides a new corpus with 59 different dialogue domains from real industrial API and a code platform to ease FSL experiment set-up, which are expected to advance the research of this field. Further, we find that insufficient performance of the few-shot setting often leads to noisy sharing between two sub-task and disturbs joint learning. To tackle this, we guide slot with explicit intent information and propose a novel trust gating mechanism that blocks low-confidence intent information to ensure high quality sharing. Besides, we introduce a Reptile-based meta-learning strategy to achieve better generalization in unseen few-shot domains. In the experiments, the proposed method brings significant improvements on two datasets and achieve new state-of-the-art performance.

The authors introduce FewJoint, a new benchmark with 59 real-world dialogue domains and an accompanying code platform for easy experiment setup. To improve noisy task sharing under few-shot conditions, they propose a trust-gating mechanism that blocks low-confidence intent signals and a Reptile-based meta-learning strategy for better generalization to unseen domains. Experiments on two datasets show significant gains and establish new state-of-the-art performance.

instruction: Write a step-by-step guide for resolving GitHub merge conflicts.
decomposed_questions: Does the generated text include steps to resolve GitHub merge conflicts?
Are the generated steps presented in a step-by-step manner?
output:
Step-by-Step Guide to Resolving GitHub Merge Conflicts

1. Pre-requisites  
   • Git installed and set up with your GitHub credentials  
   • A local clone of the repository you’re working on  
   • A feature branch (e.g. feature-branch) and a target branch (often main or develop)

2. Update Local Refs  
   • Open a terminal and cd into your repo folder  
   • Fetch the latest commits from GitHub:  
     `git fetch origin`  
   • Check out your feature branch:  
     `git checkout feature-branch`  
   • Pull any remote changes to avoid running into conflicts twice:  
     `git pull origin feature-branch`

3. Incorporate Target Branch Changes  
   You can either merge or rebase. Merging is simpler; rebasing makes a cleaner history.  
   – To merge:  
     `git merge origin/main`  
   – To rebase:  
     `git rebase origin/main`

4. Identify Conflicts  
   Git will stop and print messages like:  
     “CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in path/to/file.ext”  
   In your shell run:  
     `git status`  
   Conflicted files are listed under “both modified.”

5. Open and Resolve Conflicted Files  
   • Open each file marked as conflicted in your editor or IDE.  
   • Git places conflict markers directly in the file:  
     <<<<<<< HEAD  
       Your feature-branch code  
     =======  
       Code from main (or whatever you’re merging in)  
     >>>>>>> origin/main  
   • Decide which code to keep (or combine them).  
   • Remove the conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) after your edits.  
   • Save the file.

6. Mark Files as Resolved  
   For each file you’ve fixed run:  
     `git add path/to/file.ext`

7. Complete the Merge or Rebase  
   – If you merged:  
     `git commit`  
     Git will automatically generate a merge-commit message; you can edit it or accept it.  
   – If you rebased:  
     After all conflicts are resolved and added, continue the rebase with:  
     `git rebase --continue`

8. Test Your Changes  
   • Run your project’s test suite or perform a manual smoke test.  
   • Make sure nothing broke due to your conflict resolutions.

9. Push the Resolved Branch  
   • If you merged:  
     `git push origin feature-branch`  
   • If you rebased:  
     You may need to force-push to update the branch’s history:  
     `git push --force-with-lease origin feature-branch`

10. Finalize on GitHub  
   • Go to your Pull Request on GitHub.  
   • The conflicts should be gone and you can merge your PR.  
   • Click “Merge pull request” → “Confirm merge.”

Alternative: Resolve Conflicts in GitHub’s Web Editor  
   1. On the PR page, if conflicts are detected GitHub shows “This branch has conflicts that must be resolved.”  
   2. Click “Resolve conflicts.”  
   3. Edit directly in the browser, removing markers and choosing the correct code.  
   4. Click “Mark as resolved,” then “Commit merge.”  
   5. Finally merge the PR normally.

Tips  
   • Use a graphical mergetool (e.g. `git mergetool`) for a side-by-side view.  
   • Communicate with your team if you’re not sure which version of the code to keep.  
   • Keep commits small—resolve one conflict at a time if possible.  

You’ve now successfully resolved your merge conflicts and merged your feature into the target branch!

  Ingredients: salmon fillets, baby potatoes (halved), asparagus spears, olive oil, lemon slices, garlic powder, salt, pepper.  
  Steps: toss potatoes with oil, salt and pepper; roast at 400°F for 10 minutes. Add salmon and asparagus to the sheet pan, drizzle everything with oil, garlic powder and top salmon with lemon slices; roast 12–15 more minutes.

• Lemon-Herb Chicken and Green Beans Skillet  
  Ingredients: boneless skinless chicken breasts (or thighs), fresh green beans (trimmed), lemon zest and juice, minced garlic, dried oregano, olive oil, salt, pepper.  
  Steps: brown chicken in a large skillet with oil, remove and set aside; sauté garlic and green beans until just tender, return chicken to pan, add lemon juice, zest and oregano; simmer 5 minutes more.

• Turkey and Veggie Stir-Fry with Brown Rice  
  Ingredients: ground turkey, mixed bell peppers, snap peas or broccoli florets, grated carrot, low-sodium soy sauce, minced ginger, olive or sesame oil, cooked brown rice.  
  Steps: cook turkey until no pink remains, set aside; stir-fry veggies with oil, garlic and ginger until crisp-tender; return turkey, add soy sauce, toss and serve over rice.

• Chickpea-Spinach Coconut Curry  
  Ingredients: canned chickpeas (drained), fresh spinach, light coconut milk, diced tomatoes, curry powder, minced onion, garlic, olive oil, salt, chili flakes (optional).  
  Steps: sauté onion and garlic in oil, stir in curry powder, add tomatoes and coconut milk; simmer 5 minutes, stir in chickpeas and spinach until wilted; season and serve with cauliflower rice or whole grain naan.

• Shrimp Tacos with Quick Cabbage Slaw  
  Ingredients: peeled shrimp, taco seasoning, small corn or whole-wheat tortillas, shredded cabbage, Greek yogurt or light sour cream, lime juice, cilantro, avocado slices.  
  Steps: toss shrimp in seasoning and sauté 4–5 minutes; mix cabbage with yogurt, lime and cilantro; fill warmed tortillas with slaw, shrimp and avocado.

• Quinoa-Stuffed Bell Peppers  
  Ingredients: large bell peppers (tops cut off, seeds removed), cooked quinoa, black beans, corn kernels, diced tomatoes, shredded cheese (optional), chili powder, cumin, olive oil.  
  Steps: mix quinoa with beans, corn, tomatoes and spices; stuff peppers, top with cheese if you like; bake at 375°F for 20–25 minutes.

• One-Pot Lentil and Vegetable Soup  
  Ingredients: green or brown lentils, diced carrots, celery, onion, canned diced tomatoes, spinach or kale, vegetable broth, olive oil, thyme, bay leaf, salt, pepper.  
  Steps: sauté onion, carrot and celery in oil; add lentils, tomatoes, broth and seasonings; simmer 25 minutes, stir in greens until wilted, adjust seasoning.

instruction: Describe how to prepare the given food in your own words. Note down the ingredients you will need and the steps you will take to prepare them.

Here’s a straightforward way to make soft, chewy chocolate chip cookies.  

Ingredients  
• 2¼ cups (about 280 g) all-purpose flour  
• 1 teaspoon baking soda  
• ½ teaspoon salt  
• 1 cup (230 g) unsalted butter, at room temperature  
• ¾ cup (150 g) granulated sugar  
• ¾ cup (165 g) packed brown sugar (light or dark)  
• 1 teaspoon vanilla extract  
• 2 large eggs, at room temperature  
• 2 cups (about 340 g) semisweet chocolate chips (or chunks)  

Steps  
1. Preheat and prepare  
   • Preheat your oven to 350 °F (175 °C).  
   • Line two baking sheets with parchment paper or use a nonstick silicone mat.  

2. Mix dry ingredients  
   • In a medium bowl, whisk together the flour, baking soda, and salt. Set aside.  

3. Cream butter and sugars  
   • In a large bowl (or the bowl of a stand mixer), beat the softened butter with both sugars until the mixture is light and fluffy—about 2 to 3 minutes on medium speed.  

4. Add eggs and vanilla  
   • Crack in the eggs, one at a time, mixing well after each addition.  
   • Stir in the vanilla extract until evenly combined.  

5. Combine wet and dry  
   • Gradually add the flour mixture to the butter mixture, mixing on low speed just until no streaks of flour remain. Don’t overmix.  

6. Fold in chocolate chips  
   • Use a spatula or wooden spoon to fold in the chocolate chips evenly.  

7. Portion the dough  
   • Scoop or roll dough into balls about 1½ tablespoons each (you can use a small cookie scoop).  
   • Place them on the prepared baking sheets, spacing about 2 inches apart.  

8. (Optional) Chill for extra chewiness  
   • For even chewier cookies, cover the dough balls and chill in the refrigerator for at least 30 minutes (up to 24 hours).  

9. Bake  
   • Bake one sheet at a time in the center of the oven for 9–12 minutes, or until the edges are set but the centers still look a little soft.  

10. Cool and enjoy  
   • Let the cookies rest on the baking sheet for 5 minutes; then transfer them to a wire rack to cool completely.  
   • Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 5 days.  

Makes about 24–30 medium cookies. Enjoy warm or room temperature for that perfect chewy bite!

The task is simply to pair up every person with their address (if any), and to still list people who have no address on file.  In SQL the classic way to do this is with a LEFT OUTER JOIN:

  1. Start from the Person table — that guarantees every person will appear at least once in the result set.  
  2. LEFT JOIN the Address table on matching PersonId.  Whenever there is a row in Address with the same PersonId, its City and State columns come along.  Whenever there is no matching row in Address, the City and State columns come back as NULL.  
  3. Select exactly the four columns the problem asks for (FirstName, LastName, City, State).  

Putting it all together in SQL:

  SELECT
    P.FirstName,
    P.LastName,
    A.City,
    A.State
  FROM
    Person AS P
    LEFT JOIN Address AS A
      ON P.PersonId = A.PersonId;

This query satisfies the requirement to list every person, and to report NULL for city and state if that person has no address record.

Below is a step-by-step guide for building a very simple “pop-pop” style steam engine out of an empty aluminum beer can. This isn’t a high-pressure, high-performance model, but it does run on steam and is a classic beginner’s project. Please read all safety notes carefully before you begin.

1. Safety First  
   • Always work in a well-ventilated area, away from flammable materials.  
   • Wear safety glasses and heat-resistant gloves.  
   • Never seal the boiler completely—this design cannot handle high pressure.  
   • Keep small children and pets well clear when you first fire it up.

2. Gather Materials and Tools  
   • 1 empty, clean aluminum beer can (rinsed and dried)  
   • 2 short lengths of thin copper tubing (about 3 mm outside diameter × 15–20 mm long)  
   • Soft solder and rosin flux (or a low-temperature plumbing solder)  
   • Butane soldering iron or small propane torch  
   • Electric drill or pin vise with a 3 mm drill bit  
   • Metal snips or sharp craft knife  
   • Needle-nose pliers  
   • Small block of wood or a simple stand (optional)  
   • Water (distilled is best to reduce scale)  
   • A safe, small flame source (candle, alcohol burner or tea-light)

3. Prepare the Beer Can (Boiler)  
   a. Remove the top opening completely so you have one open end and one sealed end.  
   b. Trim off any sharp flange around the opening so it’s smooth.  
   c. On the side of the can, about 8–12 mm up from the bottom, mark two spots about 8–10 mm apart (center-to-center).

4. Drill and Fit the Tubes  
   a. Carefully drill two 3 mm holes at your marks. Keep the holes clean—remove burrs.  
   b. Slide each copper tube into a hole. They should just pass through the can wall.  
   c. Bend the tubes on the inside so they point down at a shallow angle (this gives them some rigidity and helps with seating).

5. Soldering the Tubes in Place  
   a. Apply rosin flux around each tube both inside and outside the can.  
   b. Heat gently with your torch or soldering iron until flux sizzles, then touch solder to the joint so it runs around the tube and seals the hole.  
   c. Make sure you get a good leak-tight joint—steam will escape if it’s sloppy.

6. Mounting the Boiler (Optional)  
   • You can leave the can standing on its sealed bottom, but many builders like to solder on small feet or rest it in a wooden cradle so it’s stable over the flame.  
   • If you make feet, small L-shaped tabs of copper or soldered-on nuts work fine.

7. Filling with Water  
   • Carefully pour in distilled or de-ionized water until the level is just above the lower ends of the copper tubes.  
   • A few milliliters only—too much water will extinguish your flame and too little won’t generate steam.

8. Firing Up  
   a. Place your can on its stand over your heat source.  
   b. Light the flame under the can’s bottom, concentrating the heat beneath the water level.  
   c. After a minute or so the water will start flashing to steam. You should begin to hear a rhythmic “pop-pop” sound as steam/thin water slugs are alternately expelled and drawn back in through the tubes.

9. Troubleshooting and Fine-Tuning  
   • If it never pops: check for steam leaks or clogged tubes. Make sure your water level is correct and the flame is strong enough.  
   • If it spits water but doesn’t whistle: you may need to reposition the tubes slightly downward or clear blockages.  
   • Be patient—getting the flame size, water level and tube alignment right can take a try or two.

10. Operation and Shut-Down  
    • Once you hear a steady popping, you can experiment by moving the flame closer or farther, or by gently rocking the boiler.  
    • To shut down, simply remove the heat source and let the can cool naturally. Do not cool it rapidly with water—there’s hot solder that can crack or cause steam spitting.

—  
That’s all there is to it! You now have a simple, working steam-pulse engine made from an ordinary aluminum can. Always treat it with respect—hot metal and steam can burn. Enjoy your little “pop-pop” engine, and happy tinkering!

Kale with Creamy Almond-Butter Tamari Sauce  
Serves: 2–3  
Prep time: 10 minutes  
Cook time: 10 minutes  

Ingredients  
• 1 large bunch kale (about 8–10 ounces)  
• 3 tablespoons almond butter  
• 2 tablespoons tamari  
• 2 tablespoons apple cider vinegar  
• 1 tablespoon agave nectar  
• 2–4 tablespoons water (to thin the sauce and to steam)  

Instructions  
1. Prep the kale  
   • Rinse kale leaves thoroughly and shake off excess water.  
   • Remove thick stems and tear or chop leaves into bite-sized pieces.  

2. Make the sauce  
   • In a medium bowl, combine almond butter, tamari, apple cider vinegar and agave nectar.  
   • Whisk in 2 tablespoons of water. If the dressing is very thick, add up to 2 more tablespoons of water, a little at a time, until you have a pourable but creamy sauce.  

3. Massage the kale  
   • Transfer half of the sauce to a large mixing bowl.  
   • Add the torn kale leaves and use your hands to gently massage and rub the dressing into the leaves for about 1–2 minutes. This helps soften the kale and mellow any bitterness.  

4. Cook the kale  
   • Place a large skillet or saucepan over medium heat (no oil needed).  
   • Add the dressed kale and scatter 2–3 tablespoons of water into the pan. Cover and let the kale steam for 4–5 minutes, stirring once or twice, until it’s wilted but still bright green.  

5. Finish and serve  
   • Remove the pan from heat and transfer kale to a serving platter or bowl.  
   • Drizzle with the remaining half of the almond-butter tamari sauce. Toss lightly to coat.  
   • Taste and adjust: if you’d like a touch more tang, add a splash more apple cider vinegar; for sweetness, a drizzle more agave; for saltiness, a little extra tamari.  

Serving suggestion  
Enjoy this as a stand-alone warm salad, or pair it with cooked grains (rice, quinoa) or your favorite protein if you have it on hand. The creamy, nutty sauce turns simple kale into a satisfying dinner.

input:
Mathematics and art are related in a variety of ways. Mathematics has itself been described as an art motivated by beauty. Mathematics can be discerned in arts such as music, dance, painting, architecture, sculpture, and textiles. This article focuses, however, on mathematics in the visual arts.
Mathematics and art have a long historical relationship. Artists have used mathematics since the 4th century BC when the Greek sculptor Polykleitos wrote his Canon, prescribing proportions conjectured to have been based on the ratio 1:√2 for the ideal male nude. Persistent popular claims have been made for the use of the golden ratio in ancient art and architecture, without reliable evidence. In the Italian Renaissance, Luca Pacioli wrote the influential treatise De divina proportione (1509), illustrated with woodcuts by Leonardo da Vinci, on the use of the golden ratio in art. Another Italian painter, Piero della Francesca, developed Euclid's ideas on perspective in treatises such as De Prospectiva Pingendi, and in his paintings. The engraver Albrecht Dürer made many references to mathematics in his work Melencolia I. In modern times, the graphic artist M. C. Escher made intensive use of tessellation and hyperbolic geometry, with the help of the mathematician H. S. M. Coxeter, while the De Stijl movement led by Theo van Doesburg and Piet Mondrian explicitly embraced geometrical forms. Mathematics has inspired textile arts such as quilting, knitting, cross-stitch, crochet, embroidery, weaving, Turkish and other carpet-making, as well as kilim. In Islamic art, symmetries are evident in forms as varied as Persian girih and Moroccan zellige tilework, Mughal jali pierced stone screens, and widespread muqarnas vaulting.

2. difficulty  
   – Emphasis: more general; can denote anything from minor problems to major obstacles.

3. misfortune  
   – Emphasis: bad luck or an unfortunate event rather than ongoing struggle.  
   – Usage: “suffered the misfortune of losing her luggage” (single event, unlucky).

4. trial  
   – Emphasis: a test of character or endurance, often with a connotation of moral or personal growth.

   – Emphasis: physical or mental suffering, often used in medical or emotional contexts.  
   – Usage: “pulled through her long affliction with courage” (focus on illness or pain).

Each synonym overlaps with “adversity”—meaning difficulty or misfortune—but differs in intensity, duration, scope, or connotation (e.g., whether it’s a test, a temporary setback, a disaster, or even an opportunity).

Here’s a concise overview of key periods, events, and themes in U.S. history that every student should know:

1. Pre-Columbian & Indigenous Societies  
   • Diverse Native American cultures (e.g., Iroquois, Pueblo, Mississippian)  
   • Complex trade networks, agriculture (maize), political confederacies  

2. Age of Exploration & Colonization (1492–1763)  
   • Columbus’s voyages (1492) and European rivalries (Spain, France, England)  
   • Jamestown (1607) – first permanent English settlement  
   • Plymouth Colony (1620) and Mayflower Compact—early self-government  
   • Colonial economies: tobacco in Chesapeake, plantations in the South, mixed farming and trade in New England  
   • Relations with Native Americans: alliances, trade, conflicts (Pequot War, King Philip’s War)

3. Road to Revolution (1763–1783)  
   • French and Indian War (1754–1763) expands British debt → taxation of colonies  
   • Stamp Act (1765), Townshend Acts (1767), Tea Act (1773) spark “no taxation without representation”  
   • Boston Massacre (1770), Boston Tea Party (1773)  
   • First Continental Congress (1774), Lexington and Concord (1775)  
   • Declaration of Independence (1776): natural rights, social contract  
   • Revolutionary War (1775–1783): Saratoga victory, French alliance, Yorktown surrender (1781)  
   • Treaty of Paris (1783) recognizes U.S. independence  

4. Forming a New Nation (1783–1820)  
   • Articles of Confederation: weak central government, interstate disputes  
   • Constitutional Convention (1787) → U.S. Constitution (ratified 1788)  
     – Federalism, separation of powers, Bill of Rights (1791)  
   • Washington’s presidency: Neutrality Proclamation, establishment of Cabinet, Judiciary Act (1789)  
   • Federalists vs. Democratic-Republicans (Hamilton vs. Jefferson)  
   • Louisiana Purchase (1803), Lewis & Clark Expedition (1804–1806)  
   • War of 1812: “second war of independence,” surge in nationalism  

5. Expansion & Sectional Tensions (1815–1860)  
   • “Era of Good Feelings” under Monroe, Missouri Compromise (1820)  
   • Jacksonian Democracy: universal white male suffrage, spoils system, Indian Removal (Trail of Tears, 1838)  
   • Market Revolution: canals (Erie), railroads, telegraph, factory system  
   • Second Great Awakening: reform movements (temperance, abolition, women’s rights)  
   • Texas Revolution (1836), Mexican-American War (1846–48) → Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo  
   • Compromise of 1850, Fugitive Slave Act, Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854), Bleeding Kansas  

6. Civil War & Reconstruction (1861–1877)  
   • Secession of Southern states, formation of Confederacy (1861)  
   • Major battles: Antietam (1862), Gettysburg (1863), surrender at Appomattox (1865)  
   • Emancipation Proclamation (1863), 13th Amendment (1865) abolishes slavery  
   • Reconstruction Amendments: 14th (citizenship), 15th (voting rights)  
   • Reconstruction policies, Freedmen’s Bureau, rise of Black officeholders  
   • End of Reconstruction (1877): “Redeemer” governments, Jim Crow segregation  

7. Gilded Age & Progressive Era (1877–1917)  
   • Industrialization: steel, oil, railroads, rise of tycoons (Carnegie, Rockefeller)  
   • Urbanization, immigration waves (Ellis Island, Chinese Exclusion Act 1882)  
   • Labor unrest: Knights of Labor, AFL, Pullman Strike (1894)  
   • Political corruption, patronage (“Tweed Ring”), Supreme Court’s laissez-faire stance (Lochner v. New York)  
   • Progressive reforms: trust-busting (Sherman Antitrust Act 1890), Meat Inspection Act, Women’s suffrage movement (19th Amendment, 1920)  

8. America on the World Stage (1898–1945)  
   • Spanish-American War (1898) → U.S. acquires Philippines, Puerto Rico, Guam  
   • World War I (1917–1918): Wilson’s Fourteen Points, Treaty of Versailles (U.S. Senate rejects League of Nations)  
   • Roaring Twenties: consumer culture, Jazz Age, Prohibition (18th Amendment), Harlem Renaissance  
   • Great Depression (1929–1939): stock market crash, unemployment, Dust Bowl  
   • New Deal (1933–1939): FDR’s “Three Rs” (Relief, Recovery, Reform), Social Security, SEC, WPA  
   • World War II (1941–1945): Pearl Harbor, mobilization, atomic bombs on Hiroshima/Nagasaki, United Nations founded  

9. Cold War & Civil Rights (1945–1975)  
   • Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, NATO vs. Warsaw Pact  
   • Korean War (1950–1953), Vietnam War (U.S. escalation 1964–1973)  
   • McCarthyism, Red Scare, nuclear arms race, space race (Sputnik 1957, Moon landing 1969)  
   • Civil Rights Movement: Brown v. Board (1954), Rosa Parks/Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955), March on Washington (1963), Civil Rights Act (1964), Voting Rights Act (1965)  
   • Great Society programs: Medicare, Medicaid, War on Poverty  

10. Late 20th & Early 21st Century (1975–Present)  
    • Watergate scandal, Nixon resignation (1974), “stagflation” of the 1970s  
    • Reagan Revolution: supply-side economics, end of Cold War (1989–1991)  
    • Gulf War (1990–91), NAFTA (1994), tech boom of the 1990s  
    • 9/11 attacks (2001) → War on Terror, Afghanistan and Iraq wars  
    • 2008 financial crisis, Great Recession, Affordable Care Act (2010)  
    • Recent issues: technology and social media, political polarization, debates over immigration, climate change, racial justice movements  

Key Themes to Remember  
  • Federalism vs. states’ rights  
  • Expansion and its impact on Native Americans and enslaved people  
  • Economic transformations (agrarian → industrial → digital)  
  • Waves of reform and social movements (abolition, suffrage, civil rights, environmentalism)  
  • The U.S. role in global affairs (isolationism → international leadership)

instruction:
One or more jobs can be run automatically by a workflow. The workflows are defined in the repository as YAML files and will run if an event occurs in the repository, as well as manually, or on a certain schedule.
Bring an example of a workflow that demonstrate the CI/CD features of GitHub Actions.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text an example of a workflow?
Does the generated text demonstrate the CI/CD features of GitHub Actions?
output:
Here’s a full example of a GitHub Actions workflow showing CI (build/test) and CD (Docker‐build & deploy) in one pipeline. You can drop this file in your repo at .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml:

```yaml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

# 1) when to run
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main
  workflow_dispatch:        # manual trigger
  schedule:                 # nightly run at 2 AM UTC
    - cron: '0 2 * * *'

# 2) cancel in‐flight runs on same branch
concurrency:
  group: ci-cd-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

# 3) share common env
env:
  NODE_ENV: production
  IMAGE: myrepo/myapp

jobs:

  # CI job: runs lint + test across a Node.js matrix
  test:
    name: Test & Lint (Node ${{ matrix.node }})
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node: [14.x, 16.x, 18.x]
    steps:
      - name: Checkout repo
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node.js ${{ matrix.node }}
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Lint
        run: npm run lint

      - name: Run tests with coverage
        run: npm test -- --coverage
        env:
          CI: true

      - name: Upload coverage report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: coverage-${{ matrix.node }}
          path: coverage/

  # Build job: creates a production build artifact
  build:
    name: Build Production Artifact
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout repo
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Restore coverage report from tests  # optional, just demo artifact download
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: coverage-14.x
          path: coverage/

      - name: Build app
        run: npm run build

      - name: Upload build artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: app-build
          path: build/

  # CD job #1: build & push Docker image on main
  docker:
    name: Build & Push Docker
    needs: build
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout repo
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Download build artifact
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: app-build
          path: build/

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v4
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags:
            - ${{ env.IMAGE }}:latest
            - ${{ env.IMAGE }}:${{ github.sha }}

  # CD job #2: deploy to Kubernetes (or any target)
  deploy:
    name: Deploy to Kubernetes
    needs: docker
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Setup kubectl
        uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v3
        with:
          version: 'latest'

      - name: Deploy via kubectl
        run: |
          kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
          kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp -n production
        env:
          KUBECONFIG: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_PRODUCTION }}
```

Highlights:

- Triggers on push, PRs, a nightly schedule and manual dispatch.
- `test` job runs lint & tests across a Node.js version matrix, uploads coverage artifacts.
- `build` job packages your app into a build directory.
- `docker` job builds and pushes a multi‐tag Docker image to Docker Hub (using secrets).
- `deploy` job applies your Kubernetes manifests to production.
- `concurrency` ensures only one run per branch at a time.

Here is an overview of the origin and historical development of the English word oblique:

1. Latin Roots  
   • Classical Latin obliquus “slanting, sloping, sideways, indirect”  
   • Likely built on the prefix ob- “against, in the way” plus a root meaning “bend, lean” (exact PIE source is unclear but often linked to a sense of turning or slipping)  
   • In Latin it carried both literal senses (a slanted line or posture) and figurative ones (indirect behavior or speech)

2. Passage into Old French and Middle English  
   • Old French oblique appears by the 12th century with much the same meanings  
   • Borrowed into Middle English in the 14th century (forms like obliquis, oblyqu)  
   • Early English examples often occur in geometry (“an angle that is not right”) and in moral or rhetorical contexts (“an oblique answer,” meaning not straightforward)

3. Semantic Extensions in English  
   • 14th–15th centuries: “slanting” or “tilted” in physical/geometric senses  
   • By late 14th century: figurative sense “indirect, devious, not straightforward”  
   • 16th–17th centuries: extended to “cast a sidelong glance” or “apply in a slanted way”  
   • Early 18th century: grammatical use in “oblique case,” meaning any case other than the nominative

4. Related Forms and Cognates  
   • English derivatives: obliquely (adv), obliqueness or obliquity (n)  
   • Romance cognates: French oblique, Spanish oblicuo, Italian obliquo, Portuguese oblíquo  
   • All trace back to the same Latin obliquus root

5. Key Points in Its History  
   • Originates in Latin as a compound suggesting “turned aside” or “in the way”  
   • Enters English via Old French, first in technical (geometry) and then in figurative contexts  
   • Develops a wide range of abstract senses—indirect speech or conduct, grammatical case, typographic style (sometimes “oblique” in print to mean slanted type)  

Over roughly eight centuries the word carried its central notion of “not straight” from physical tilts in ancient Rome through medieval geometry and into our modern uses for anything indirect, slanted, or non-perpendicular.

Here are some practical tips to help you stay calm and confident during class presentations:

1. Prepare Thoroughly  
   • Research your topic well so you feel confident about the content.  
   • Organize your material into a clear structure (introduction, main points, conclusion).  
   • Create concise note cards or an outline to guide you—having a roadmap reduces anxiety.

2. Practice Out Loud  
   • Rehearse your presentation multiple times, speaking as if you’re in front of the class.  
   • Time yourself to ensure you stay within the allotted slot.  
   • Practice in front of a friend, family member, or record yourself to spot areas for improvement.

3. Visualize Success  
   • Spend a few minutes before your talk imagining the presentation going smoothly.  
   • Picture yourself speaking clearly, engaging the audience, and finishing on a strong note.  
   • Positive visualization can rewire your brain away from “what if something goes wrong.”

4. Use Deep Breathing Techniques  
   • Inhale slowly through your nose for a count of four, hold for two, and exhale for a count of six.  
   • Repeat this cycle two or three times just before you begin.  
   • Deep breathing lowers heart rate and calms jittery nerves.

5. Start with a Strong, Prepared Opening  
   • Memorize or practice your first few lines until they feel natural—getting off to a confident start sets the tone.  
   • Consider a brief anecdote, question, or surprising fact to engage your listeners right away.

6. Focus on Message, Not Yourself  
   • Shift attention from “How am I doing?” to “What am I trying to teach or convey?”  
   • Remind yourself that the audience is there to learn from you, not to judge you.

7. Make Eye Contact and Engage the Audience  
   • Look at friendly faces or scan the room in three sections (left, center, right).  
   • Smiling and nodding at audience reactions can boost your confidence.

8. Embrace Natural Pauses  
   • Short pauses give you time to think and break up nervous speech patterns.  
   • Silence can feel longer to you than to the audience—use it strategically before key points.

9. Keep Notes Handy  
   • Having a few bullet points on your slides or note cards serves as a safety net.  
   • If you lose your place, refer to your notes calmly rather than panicking.

10. Reflect and Learn  
   • After your presentation, jot down what went well and what you’d like to improve.  
   • Celebrate small wins (clear voice, good eye contact, smooth transitions) to build confidence for next time.

Bonus Self-Care Tips  
   • Get a good night’s sleep before your presentation.  
   • Avoid excessive caffeine or sugar right before speaking.  
   • Do a quick walk or light stretch to release tension.

By combining solid preparation with calming techniques and a mindset shift toward your message, you can significantly reduce nerves and deliver a more confident, engaging presentation. Good luck!

Here’s a concise, efficient Python function with type hints and a doc-string that tests primality by trial division up to √n, skipping even numbers and multiples of 3:

```python
import math

def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    """
    Determine whether an integer is prime.

    Args:
        n (int): The number to test.

    Returns:
        bool: True if n is prime, False otherwise.

    Raises:
        TypeError: If n is not an integer.
    """
    if not isinstance(n, int):
        raise TypeError(f"Expected int, got {type(n).__name__}")

    # Exclude numbers less than 2
    if n < 2:
        return False
    # 2 and 3 are prime
    if n in (2, 3):
        return True
    # Exclude multiples of 2 or 3
    if n % 2 == 0 or n % 3 == 0:
        return False

    # Check divisibility by numbers of form 6k ± 1 up to sqrt(n)
    limit = int(math.isqrt(n))
    i = 5
    while i <= limit:
        if n % i == 0 or n % (i + 2) == 0:
            return False
        i += 6
    return True
```

Usage examples:

print(is_prime(2))    # True

Here’s a simple, no-bake vegan dessert that comes together in minutes: a rich Chocolate-Avocado Mousse.  

Yields: 2–4 servings  
Prep time: 10 minutes  
Chill time (optional): 20–30 minutes  

Ingredients  
• 2 ripe avocados, peeled and pitted  
• ¼ cup (25 g) unsweetened cocoa powder  
• ¼–½ cup (60–120 ml) plant-based milk (almond, oat, soy, etc.)  
• 3–4 tablespoons (45–60 ml) maple syrup or agave nectar (to taste)  
• 1 teaspoon vanilla extract  
• Pinch of fine sea salt  

Optional toppings  
• Fresh berries (raspberries, strawberries, blueberries)  
• Toasted coconut flakes  
• Chopped nuts (pistachios, almonds, hazelnuts)  
• Vegan whipped cream or coconut cream  
• A few fresh mint leaves  

Steps  
1. Prepare the avocados: halve each avocado, remove the pit, and scoop the flesh into a blender or food processor.  
2. Add the cocoa and sweetener: pour in the cocoa powder, maple syrup (start with 3 Tbsp), vanilla, salt, and half of your plant milk.  
3. Blend to creamy: process on high until smooth. If it’s too thick, add the remaining milk a tablespoon at a time until you reach your desired consistency.  
4. Taste and adjust: sample the mousse, adding more sweetener or a touch more cocoa if you prefer it darker. Blend again briefly.  
5. Chill (optional): scrape the mousse into small serving bowls or glasses and refrigerate for 20–30 minutes—it firms up beautifully—but you can also serve it right away.  
6. Garnish & serve: top each portion with berries, coconut flakes, nuts or a dollop of vegan cream and enjoy.  

Variations  
• Espresso kick: add ½ tsp instant espresso powder for mocha flavor.  
• Mint chocolate: drop in a few fresh mint leaves with the other ingredients.  
• Nut-butter swirl: swirl in 1–2 Tbsp of peanut or almond butter before chilling.  

This mousse is ultra-creamy, naturally sweetened, and packs healthy fats from the avocado. Enjoy!

Here’s a quick tip on verb endings in German:

1. Infinitive ending  
   – Almost all German verbs in their dictionary (infinitive) form end in -en (z. B. spielen, machen). A few end in -n (e.g. tun).

2. Present‐tense conjugation  
   – Take the verb stem (Infinitiv minus -en) and add these endings:  
     • ich ‑e  
     • du ‑st  
     • er/sie/es ‑t  
     • wir ‑en  
     • ihr ‑t  
     • sie/Sie ‑en  

3. Extra “e” for stems ending in -t or -d  
   – If the stem ends in -t, -d, -fn, -gn, -chn oder -tm, insert an extra “e” before the ‑st and ‑t so it’s easier to pronounce:  
     • du arbeitest, er wartet  

That way you always know how to “end” your German verbs correctly!

Here’s a quick step-by-step guide to uploading and using a bibliography database (.bib) in Overleaf:

1. Prepare your .bib file  
   • On your computer, create or export your bibliography in BibTeX format and save it as, for example, `references.bib`.

2. Log in and open your Overleaf project  
   • Go to overleaf.com, sign in, and either create a new project or open an existing one.

3. Upload the .bib file  
   • In the Overleaf file tree (left side), click the “Upload” button (an upward-pointing arrow).  
   • Drag & drop your `references.bib` file or click to browse and select it.

4. Include the bibliography in your LaTeX document  
   • If you’re using the traditional BibTeX workflow, in your main `.tex` file add near the end:
       \bibliographystyle{plain}      % or another style like alpha, IEEEtran, etc.  
       \bibliography{references}      % omit the “.bib” extension  
   • If you prefer biblatex+biber, in your preamble write:
       \usepackage[backend=biber,style=alphabetic]{biblatex}  
       \addbibresource{references.bib}  

5. Cite entries in your text  
   • Use \cite{<BibTeXKey>} where `<BibTeXKey>` is the identifier you gave each entry in `references.bib`.

6. Compile your document  
   • Hit “Recompile.” Overleaf will run LaTeX → BibTeX (or Biber) → LaTeX twice to resolve references.  
   • Check the PDF preview: your bibliography should appear at the place you put `\bibliography` or `\printbibliography`.

That’s it! Your bibliography database is now uploaded and ready to be cited in your Overleaf project.

instruction: Verify the correctness of the given statement.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text a judgment of the correctness of a statement?
Is the judgment of correctness in the generated text reasonable for the statement in the given input?
output:
The statement “For all integers j and k, if j and k are odd, then jk is odd” is true.  Here is a direct proof:

1. By hypothesis, j and k are odd integers.  
2. By definition of odd, there exist integers m and n such that  
   j = 2m + 1  
   k = 2n + 1  
3. Multiply:  
   jk = (2m + 1)(2n + 1)  
      = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1  
      = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1  
4. Since (2mn + m + n) is an integer, jk has the form 2·(integer) + 1, i.e. jk is odd.

Thus the original implication holds for all integers j and k.

Statement: "For every integer k, k^2 + 2k + 1 ≥ 0"
Fact: The square of any real number is non-negative.
instruction: Based on the facts that have been provided, prove the following statement.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text a proof?

Does the proof in the generated text use the facts in the given input?
Is the proof in the generated text valid?
output:
Proof. Let k be an arbitrary integer.  Then k+1 is a real number, so by the given fact its square is non‐negative:  
    (k+1)² ≥ 0.  
But expanding the square gives  
    (k+1)² = k² + 2k + 1.  
Hence for every integer k we have  
    k² + 2k + 1 = (k+1)² ≥ 0,  
as was to be shown.

input:
How do I compare strings in Java?
I've been using the == operator in my program to compare all my strings so far. However, I ran into a bug, changed one of them into .equals() instead, and it fixed the bug.
Is == bad? When should it and should it not be used? What's the difference?
instruction: Answer the following question.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text a question answer?
Does the generated text provide an answer to all the questions in the given input?
Does the answer in the generated text accurate for the question in the given input?
output:
In Java, String is an object, so using == and using .equals(…) do two very different things:

1. “==” checks whether two references point at the *exact same* object in memory  
   • You can get “== true” only if both variables refer to the same String instance (for example, two references to the same interned literal).  
   • You will get “== false” even if the two Strings hold identical characters, as long as they aren’t the very same object.

2. str1.equals(str2) checks whether two String *objects* contain the same sequence of characters  
   • This is almost always what you want when you “compare” strings.  
   • equals() is overridden in java.lang.String to compare the character data, not the references.

When to use which?

• Always use .equals(...) (or .equalsIgnoreCase(...)) when you want to test whether two strings have the same text.  
• Only use == when you really mean “are these two references pointing to the same object?” (for instance, when you’re doing very low-level optimizations or when comparing enum values).  
• If you ever worry about one of the variables being null, you can either do a null check first or use Objects.equals(a, b) (returns false if either is null, true only if both are non-null and equal).

Extras:

• To compare strings lexicographically (i.e. for sorting), use str1.compareTo(str2) (returns <0 if str1<str2, 0 if equal, >0 if str1>str2).  
• For case-insensitive content comparison, use str1.equalsIgnoreCase(str2).  

Example:
```java
String a = "hello";
String b = new String("hello");
String c = "hello";

System.out.println(a == b);          // false  (different objects)
System.out.println(a.equals(b));     // true   (same characters)
System.out.println(a == c);          // true   (both point to the interned literal "hello")

if (userInput.equals("quit")) {
  // correct way to test for the text “quit”
}
```

Project Idea: “Upcycled Motherboard LED Smart Clock”  
Turn an old, dead PC motherboard and scrap electronics into a one-of-a-kind wall clock that uses addressable LEDs to tell the time—and looks amazing doing it. This project uses only low-voltage electronics (5 V), is completely safe if you follow normal soldering and drilling precautions, and gives new life to e-waste.

Materials & Tools  
• Old ATX motherboard (any non-working board will do)  
• Salvaged ESP8266 or Arduino-compatible board (e.g. NodeMCU from a broken IoT device)  
• WS2812 (NeoPixel) LED ring (12–24 LEDs) rescued from damaged LED décor or strip  
• 5 V power supply (USB phone charger, power-bank electronics, or salvaged USB cable)  
• Small length of hookup wire, solder, heat-shrink tubing  
• Clear acrylic diffuser (scrap from a broken display or picture frame)  
• Mounting hardware (stand-offs, screws)  
• Drill with bits, flush cutters, screwdriver, soldering iron, safety glasses, gloves  
• Optional: battery pack from old phone as backup power  

Step-by-Step Instructions

1. Prepare & Clean the Motherboard  
  a. Remove all loose components (plastic headers, fan connectors) that might get in the way  
  b. Wipe off dust/grime with isopropyl alcohol; let it dry fully  

2. Plan Your Layout  
  a. Decide where the LED ring will sit—typically centered over the CPU socket or chipset heatsink  
  b. Mark the mounting holes or a cut-out for the ring’s center on the board with a pencil  

3. Cut & Drill  
  a. Drill small pilot holes at your mounting points, then enlarge to fit your standoffs or screws  
  b. If the LED ring sits inset, use a hole saw or step bit to cut a circular recess behind it (optional)  
  c. Deburr all holes; wear gloves and goggles  

4. Wire Up the LED Ring & Controller  
  a. Cut three wires (5 V, GND, data) to length; strip and tin the ends  
  b. Solder wires to the LED ring’s 5 V, GND, and data-in pads  
  c. Solder the other ends to the ESP8266/Arduino board (5 V → VIN or 5 V pin; GND → GND; Data → a digital I/O pin, e.g. D5)  
  d. Insulate all joints with heat-shrink or tape  

5. Program the Microcontroller  
  a. Install Arduino IDE (or your preferred environment) and add the Adafruit_NeoPixel (or FastLED) library  
  b. Load or write a simple clock sketch that:  
     • Initializes the LED ring,  
     • Retrieves time via NTP (requires Wi-Fi credentials in code),  
     • Maps hours/minutes to LED positions (e.g. LED 0–11 = hours, LED 12–23 = minutes or seconds),  
     • Updates the ring once per second/minute  
  c. Upload the code and test on your bench before assembly  

6. Build the Power Supply  
  a. If using a USB charger or power bank module, mount it behind the motherboard so it feeds the controller’s 5 V line  
  b. Secure all wires; avoid any chance they can short to motherboard traces  

7. Mount Everything Together  
  a. Fasten the motherboard to a backing board (plywood or acrylic) using standoffs  
  b. Clip or screw the LED ring in place so it protrudes just above the motherboard surface  
  c. Attach the ESP8266/Arduino to one corner with double-sided tape or standoffs  
  d. If you have acrylic as a diffuser, cut it to match the motherboard outline and glue it over the LEDs  

8. Final Assembly & Testing  
  a. Plug in the 5 V supply and let your smart clock boot  
  b. Watch the LED ring light up, sync to Wi-Fi, and begin keeping time  
  c. Tidy wires and perform a final safety check—ensure no exposed solder or sharp edges  

9. Mount on the Wall  
  a. Hang it like any picture frame, or add keyhole slots on the back  
  b. Enjoy the conversation starter—and the fact that you rescued e-waste from landfill!  

Tips & Variations  
• Swap the LED ring for a strip of 60 LEDs and use two pins on the board to show hours vs. minutes.  
• Paint or silk-screen simple hour markers onto the motherboard surface with enamel paint.  
• Use a salvaged 18650 battery pack for battery-backup and add a charging module.  
• Turn it into a “word clock” by wiring up small matrix LEDs to spell out “It is five past ten,” etc.  

Safety Notes  
• Always work at low voltage (5 V). Do not cut into any of the motherboard’s high-voltage sections (ATX power socket, big capacitors).  
• Wear eye protection when drilling or cutting board material.  
• Be careful with soldering irons and hot melt glue guns.  
• Unplug the power before making any wiring changes.  

With this project you’ve saved a motherboard, an ESP8266/Arduino board, and some decorative LEDs from the trash, and turned them into a fully functional, Wi-Fi-enabled clock. Good luck in the contest!

Challenge Name  
EveryBody100K: 100 Kilometers in 10 Days

Overview  
Invite everyone—runners, walkers, cyclists, swimmers, hikers—to accumulate 100 km (or 62 mi) of movement in any combination of activities over a 10-day window. It’s simple, flexible, and suitable for all fitness levels.

Duration  
• 10 consecutive days (pick any 10-day block, e.g. May 1–10)  
• You don’t have to record every day; you just need to hit 100 km total by Day 10.

How to Join  
1. Create or log into your Strava account.  
2. Search for the “EveryBody100K” club and click JOIN.  
3. Post a “Let’s go!” message in the club feed with the hashtag #EveryBody100K.

Goal  
• 100 km total of any Strava-recorded activities in 10 days.

Allowed Activities  
• Running, walking, hiking, cycling, swimming, rowing, skiing, indoor training—anything you track on Strava.  
• Mix and match as you like; 5 km run + 20 km ride + 3 km swim all count toward your 100 km.

Rules  
1. All distance must be recorded on Strava. If Strava doesn’t auto-record your swim or row, you can manually upload as long as distance is clear.  
2. Each session must be at least 5 minutes long to count.  
3. No single day distance limit—you can knock out 50 km in one long ride if you like—but you must finish the 100 km by Day 10.  
4. Keep it honest and have fun—no cheating on distances.

Tracking & Social  
• Use the hashtag #EveryBody100K on every activity so everyone can cheer you on.  
• Post mid-challenge updates (“Day 5: 48 km done!”) in the club feed with a photo or screenshot.  
• Give virtual kudos to fellow participants when you see their progress.

Mini-Challenges (optional week-in-week-out prompts)  
• Day 1–3: Try a new route.  
• Day 4–6: Sneak in a sunrise or sunset session.  
• Day 7–9: Partner up—find a buddy or virtual friend.  
• Last day: Go out with a smile—take a photo at your favorite spot.

Prizes & Recognition  
• All finishers get a digital “EveryBody100K Finisher” badge in the club.  
• Top 10 most creative photo captions win a custom “Strava Star” virtual medal.  
• A special shout-out in the club newsletter to everyone who reaches 100 km.

Tips for Success  
• Break it down: 100 km ÷ 10 days = 10 km/day on average, or 20 km every other day—mix walking and cycling if 10 km runs feel tough.  
• Schedule: put short/mid-length sessions on busy days, long ones on free days.  
• Celebrate small wins: treat yourself when you hit 25 km, 50 km, 75 km.

Ready, set, go! Gather your friends, family, co-workers—everyone can join the EveryBody100K challenge. See you in the club!

It began on a warm summer evening in Amsterdam, just days before the Dutch national team was to kick off its first “OneLove” fixture against Belgium. In the cavernous press hall at the Johan Cruyff Arena, ten captains—representing the Netherlands, England, Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and Wales—stood side by side beneath a huge banner: a mosaic heart woven from ten national flags. There was Teun van Dijk of the Netherlands, whose grandfather had been a refugee; Emma Kerr of England, whose mother had the first disability football club in Manchester; Rik De Smet of Belgium, who’d organized street games in Brussels for migrant children; and France’s Laura Dupont, who’d long campaigned against anti-Semitism in sport. Each player had a personal story to share—stories of overcoming prejudice and building unity—and each was ready to spend an entire season turning those stories into action.

Over the next nine months, every home fixture for these ten teams became a OneLove event. In Copenhagen, Denmark’s Lars Christiansen swapped his captain’s armband for a rainbow-stitched version and invited a choir of young Syrian refugees to sing the national anthem before kickoff. In Hamburg, Germany’s Kai Müller hosted a “Football Without Walls” clinic for LGBT+ teens and people with disabilities, letting them train on the same turf where the Bundesliga giants practiced. In Oslo, Norway’s Ingrid Bjørnsdottir led a panel discussion—live-streamed to fans across Europe—on how to stamp out sexism in stadiums. Sweden’s Mikael Johansson partnered with migrant-run street teams in Malmö to hold an art competition: the winners’ designs later appeared on one of the official OneLove scarves. In Wales, Dylan Hughes and his teammates visited a prison outside Cardiff to coach inmates in teamwork and respect, then invited them as honored guests to the next international friendly.

Behind the scenes, UEFA coordinated a rolling “OneLove Trophy” tour. Every month it traveled to a different capital—Brussels, London, Bern, Paris—where federations hosted community fairs, family football days and fundraising dinners. Proceeds went to ten grassroots organizations, one per country, each dedicated to combating a specific form of discrimination: anti-Roma bias in Sweden, homophobia in France, xenophobia in Switzerland, ableism in England, and so on. Fan clubs across Europe mounted bus trips, bringing stand-up banners reading “One Pitch, One People” in Polish, Arabic, Turkish, Welsh and Frisian. Social-media challenges spread rapidly: supporters posted short videos calling out discrimination whenever they saw it, tagging #OneLove and nominating their friends—soon hundreds of thousands of pledges had been made.

The season climaxed in Paris, where all ten teams joined forces for the “OneLove All-Stars” exhibition at the sold-out Stade de France. Fans flooded in wearing multi-colored scarves; the giant screens aired pre-recorded testimonials from refugee families, LGBTQ+ activists and disability-rights leaders. When the players emerged, each team’s captain raised a single white jersey stitched with the names of every participating nation. The match itself ended in a thrilling 4–4 draw, but the final whistle mattered little: in the post-game embrace, rivals from ten countries stood shoulder to shoulder, forming a human chain that stretched across the pitch, lit by rainbow-colored fireworks. 

By season’s end, OneLove had achieved more than any single federation could alone. National leagues adopted new anti-discrimination codes, youth academies across Europe introduced mandatory inclusion workshops, and fan organizations created permanent “OneLove Committees.” More than two million people had signed the campaign’s online pledge; dozens of new community-based teams—mixing genders, backgrounds and abilities—emerged in towns from Lille to Ljubljana. And somewhere in a refugee camp outside Hamburg, a small group of children played the beautiful game beneath the banner of OneLove, dreaming that one day they too might wear a national jersey—knowing that football, at its best, belongs to everyone.

instruction: Give me an idea of the mental exercises you do to inspire yourself.
decomposed_questions: Does the generated text include some mental exercises?
Are the mental exercises in the generated text useful to insiper people?
output:
Here are a few mental-exercise techniques you can try to kick-start fresh ideas and keep yourself inspired. Think of them as “workouts for the mind”:

•  Mind-Mapping  
  – Pick a central theme or problem, write it in the middle of a page, then draw branches out to related words, questions, oppositions or images. Keep branching as long as you can—connections often spark unexpected insights.

•  Free Association Chain  
  – Start with one random word (say, “window”), then jot down whatever word that word makes you think of next, and so on. After a dozen links, examine the chain for surprising leaps that could become creative angles.

•  SCAMPER Checklist  
  – SCAMPER stands for Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other uses, Eliminate, Reverse. Take an existing idea or challenge and systematically apply each prompt (“What if I substitute X for Y?” “What if I reversed the process?”).

•  Six Thinking Hats (by Edward de Bono)  
  – Role-play six perspectives: logical facts (White), emotions (Red), critical judgment (Black), optimistic benefits (Yellow), creative alternatives (Green), and process control (Blue). Shifting hats helps you see an issue from multiple sides.

•  Random-Input Technique  
  – Flip through a magazine or app, pick a random image or word, and force yourself to link it to your current problem. Surprising inputs often jolt you out of habitual thinking.

•  Visual Meditation / Mental Movies  
  – Close your eyes and imagine a scenario related to your challenge—focus on colors, textures, sounds. Let details emerge without censorship. Afterwards, sketch or describe what you saw; you may uncover overlooked angles.

•  “What If?” Questions  
  – Break assumptions by asking “What if money didn’t matter?” “What if people could teleport?” or “What if this problem were caused by X instead of Y?” Outlandish premises can yield surprisingly practical ideas once you reel them back in.

•  Morphological Chart  
  – List all the key dimensions or attributes of your project in rows (e.g., shape, color, material, user group) and brainstorm multiple options for each. Then mix-and-match cells to generate combinations you hadn’t considered.

•  Dialogue with an Imaginary Mentor  
  – Picture someone you admire (real or fictional) and mentally ask them advice on your challenge. How would they frame the question? What solutions might they propose?

•  Five Whys  
  – To dive deeper into any problem, ask “Why?” five times in succession. This uncovers root causes or hidden needs that can become fertile ground for creativity.

Pick one or two of these each day, spend 5–10 minutes on them, and you’ll gradually build a habit of playful, disciplined thinking that keeps inspiration flowing.

Here’s a quick, no-equipment office routine you can knock out in 5–7 minutes. Move from one exercise to the next with minimal rest—repeat once if you have extra time.

1. Warm-Up (30 seconds)  
   • March or jog in place, swinging your arms to get blood moving.

2. Desk Push-Ups (30–45 seconds)  
   • Hands shoulder-width on desk or countertop; body in a straight line; lower chest toward desk, then press back up.

3. Chair Squats (15 reps)  
   • Stand in front of your chair, feet hip-width. Sit back gently until your glutes touch the seat, then stand tall.

4. Seated Leg Raises (10 reps per leg)  
   • Sit tall at edge of chair. Extend one leg straight out and hold 2–3 sec, then switch.

5. Standing Calf Raises (20 reps)  
   • Hold chair-back for balance, rise onto toes fully, lower down with control.

6. Desk Plank (30 seconds)  
   • Place forearms on desk, step back so your body forms a straight line from head to heels.

7. Glute Squeezes (30 seconds)  
   • While seated, squeeze cheeks together, hold 2–3 sec, release—repeat.

8. Upper-Body Stretch (30 seconds)  
   • Shoulder rolls (10 forward, 10 back), then gentle neck tilts side to side.

Feel free to tweak reps or times to match your fitness level. Even a few rounds spread through the day’ll help combat stiffness and boost energy.
