input: The "fair trade" movement, also known as the "trade justice" movement, promotes the use of labour, environmental and social standards for the production of commodities, particularly those exported from the Third and Second Worlds to the First World. Such ideas have also sparked a debate on whether trade itself should be codified as a human right.
instruction: Improve the article using your knowledge of the topic in order to make it more informative.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text an article?
Does the generated text talk about the topic of the article in the given input?
Does the generated text have additional information compared to the article in the given input?
output:
Fair Trade (also known as the Trade Justice Movement) is a global social movement and market‐based approach aimed at ensuring that producers in Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean receive a fair price for their goods, work under decent labour conditions, and contribute to sustainable development. Over the past three decades Fair Trade has grown from small specialty‐product networks into a worldwide system with multiple certification schemes, hundreds of producer‐owned cooperatives and buying organizations, and annual global sales in excess of ten billion U.S. dollars.

1. Historical Background  
• Origins in the 1940s and 1950s arose from church and development agency efforts to help marginal producers in the Colonial World find stable markets.  
• The modern Fair Trade movement crystallized in 1988 with the founding of Stichting Max Havelaar in the Netherlands, the first independent Fair Trade certification and labeling organization.  
• In 1997 several national labeling initiatives formed Fairtrade Labelling Organizations International (FLO), later rebranded as Fairtrade International, to harmonize standards and licensing.  

2. Core Principles and Standards  
Fair Trade certification schemes—such as Fairtrade International, the World Fair Trade Organization (WFTO), and Rainforest Alliance—apply a set of social, economic and environmental criteria including:  
• A minimum price floor that covers the cost of sustainable production.  
• An additional Fair Trade premium enabling community development projects (schools, health clinics, infrastructure).  
• Guaranteed pre‐financing or credit facilities for smallholders.  
• Prohibitions on forced or child labour and requirements for safe working conditions.  
• Support for democratic organization and capacity building in producer cooperatives.  
• Environmental protections including restrictions on agrochemicals, encouragement of organic farming and water conservation practices.  

3. Key Commodities and Markets  
• Coffee and cocoa remain the largest Fair Trade product categories.  
• Other certified products include tea, sugar, bananas, flowers, spices, honey, nuts, cotton, wine, sports balls and handicrafts.  
• Main consumer markets are the European Union, North America, Japan and increasingly Australia and China.  

4. Organizational Structures  
• Fairtrade International sets global standards, certifies producer organizations and authorizes independent labeling bodies in each market country.  
• The World Fair Trade Organization (WFTO) operates on a membership basis to guarantee that 100% of an organization’s turnover is Fair Trade.  
• Local and transnational NGOs, faith‐based groups, ethical traders and alternative trading organizations (ATOs) help with marketing, technical assistance and advocacy.  

5. Impact Assessment  
Research suggests Fair Trade can:  
• Increase producer incomes, bolster resilience to price volatility, and support community social infrastructure.  
• Encourage environmentally friendly practices and reduce pesticide use.  
• Raise consumer awareness of global inequalities and foster solidarity.  
However, outcomes vary by region and sector; some studies highlight limited reach to the poorest farmers and challenges in scaling up.  

6. Criticisms and Controversies  
• Certification costs and complex procedures may exclude the smallest or most remote producers.  
• Minimum price mechanisms can distort local markets or disincentivize quality improvement when global prices rise above the Fair Trade floor.  
• Questions remain about audit transparency, the share of retail premium passing to farmers, and competition with other ethical labels.  

7. Trade as a Human Right Debate  
Building on Article 23 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (right to work, free choice of employment and just remuneration), and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, some scholars and activists argue for enshrining the right “to engage in fair and equitable international trade” as a human right. Proponents contend that guaranteeing non‐discriminatory market access and decent trading terms is essential to dignity and development. Opponents warn that codifying trade rights could undermine state sovereignty in economic policy and conflict with multilateral trade agreements.  

8. Future Directions  
• Integration of Fair Trade principles into mainstream corporate supply chains beyond niche markets.  
• Digital traceability and blockchain for greater transparency in origin, pricing and certification.  
• Strengthening South–South Fair Trade networks.  
• Advocacy for stronger environmental and climate‐resilience criteria in certification.  

Conclusion  
Fair Trade has moved from a marginal alternative‐trade network to a recognized mechanism for poverty alleviation, sustainable agriculture and ethical consumption. While it cannot address all structural inequities in global commerce, its principles and practices continue to influence policies, corporate codes of conduct and consumer expectations about how goods should be produced and traded.

Here are some reasons why Barcelona is well worth a visit:

• Architectural marvels  
  – Antoni Gaudí’s masterpieces (Sagrada Família, Park Güell, Casa Batlló) blend imagination, color and light in ways you won’t find anywhere else.  
  – The Gothic Quarter offers narrow medieval streets, hidden plazas and centuries-old buildings that feel like stepping back in time.

• Rich cultural life  
  – World-class museums (Picasso Museum, MNAC, MACBA) showcase Catalan and international art.  
  – Frequent festivals and street performances fill the city with music, dance and local traditions year-round.

• Mediterranean beaches and promenade  
  – Over four kilometers of sandy shore for sunbathing, swimming or beach volleyball.  
  – A lively waterfront lined with restaurants and cafés—perfect for sipping horchata or sampling fresh seafood.

• Outstanding gastronomy  
  – Tapas bars, bustling markets (La Boqueria), Michelin-starred restaurants and hidden tapas alleys cater to every palate.  
  – Catalan specialties like pa amb tomàquet, fideuà and crema catalana offer a delicious local twist.

• Green spaces and scenic viewpoints  
  – Montjuïc and Tibidabo hills provide panoramic city vistas, botanical gardens, historic fortresses and Olympic sites.  
  – Ciutadella Park is ideal for picnics, paddle-boating and watching the iconic Cascada fountain.

• Vibrant nightlife and live music  
  – From intimate jazz clubs and flamenco tablaos to trendy rooftop bars and beachfront clubs, there’s something for every mood.  
  – Late-night tapas crawls keep the city buzzing until dawn.

• Easy access to day trips  
  – The monastery of Montserrat, the modernist town of Sitges, the vineyards of Penedès and the Costa Brava’s picturesque coves are all within easy reach.

In my view, Barcelona’s seamless mix of art, history, beach and culinary delights makes it a city that continually surprises and inspires. Whether you’re strolling through winding alleys, savoring local flavors or relaxing by the sea, you’ll quickly see why Barcelona is a must-visit destination.

output:
Here are some easy ways to celebrate more sustainably:

1. Choose eco-friendly decorations  
   • Use LED string lights—they use up to 80% less energy and last longer.  
   • Swap disposable tinsel and plastic ornaments for natural items like dried citrus, cinnamon sticks or wooden decorations.  
   • Repurpose or upcycle items you already have before buying new décor.

2. Wrap gifts responsibly  
   • Use reusable fabric wraps (Furoshiki) or scarves—no tape needed, and they look beautiful.  
   • Reuse gift bags, ribbons and bows from past years.  
   • If you prefer paper, choose recycled wrapping paper printed with eco-friendly inks.

3. Select thoughtful, low-impact gifts  
   • Opt for experiences (museum passes, classes, memberships) instead of physical items.  
   • Give consumables like fair-trade chocolate, organic tea or locally made preserves.  
   • Support small businesses, artisans and charities.

4. Reduce food waste  
   • Plan your menu and portions in advance.  
   • Shop local and seasonal ingredients to cut down on food miles.  
   • Turn leftovers into soups, stews or casseroles—and compost scraps.

5. Travel more sustainably  
   • Carpool, use public transit or rideshare when heading to holiday gatherings.  
   • If flying, consider offsetting your carbon emissions through reputable programs.  
   • For longer stays, choose eco-certified accommodations or green-friendly rentals.

6. Use energy wisely  
   • Unplug holiday lights and appliances when you’re not using them.  
   • Set timers on indoor and outdoor décor lighting.  
   • Lower your thermostat a few degrees and bundle up with cozy sweaters and blankets.

7. Trim a tree thoughtfully  
   • If you love a real tree, buy from a local, sustainably managed tree farm and recycle it after the season.  
   • An artificial tree can be greener if you already own one—just keep using it for 8–10 years to offset its production footprint.  
   • Consider a living potted tree you can replant or keep long-term.

8. Give back to the planet  
   • Make a donation in someone’s name to an environmental charity.  
   • Volunteer for a local cleanup or tree-planting event over the holidays.  
   • Plant native flowers or shrubs in your yard to support pollinators.

By making a few small swaps, you’ll not only lower your environmental impact but also inspire friends and family to celebrate greener holidays year after year. Happy eco-friendly festivities!

2. Pop your corn as usual (oil or air-popper – both work).

Finally! After a while of shooting in the dark and frantically fiddling with sample inputs on the whiteboard, you've came up with an algorithm for solving the coding question your interviewer gave you.
Whew. Such a relief to have a clear path forward. To not be flailing anymore.
Now you're cruising, getting ready to code up your solution.
When suddenly, your interviewer throws you a curve ball.
"What if we thought of the problem this way?"
You feel a tension we've all felt during the coding interview:
"Try to listen to what they're saying...but don't lose your train of thought...ugh, I can't do both!"
instruction: You will need to guide this person through the scenario they have described for the interview.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text a guide?

Is the guide in the generated text helpful for the scenario in the given input?
output:
Here’s a step-by-step approach you can use whenever your interviewer tosses you a new angle mid-solution—so you stay calm, stay engaged, and keep your momentum:

1. Pause and Breathe  
   • Take a micro-pause (a deep breath or a single “hm!”) to reset your mental state.  
   • This brief moment clears away the “frantic coding” haze and lets you focus on the new prompt.

2. Actively Listen and Paraphrase  
   • Look at the interviewer and say: “Got it—you’d like to reconsider the problem so that we do X instead of Y, right?”  
   • Paraphrasing shows you’re paying attention and ensures you’ve captured their new requirement correctly.

3. Ask Clarifying Questions  
   • “Does this new perspective affect the input constraints (size, sorting, duplicates)?”  
   • “Is the expected output format or performance target still the same?”  
   • These questions help you scope the change precisely and avoid wasted work.

4. Map the Change onto Your Existing Plan  
   • Mentally (or briefly on the board) draw your original approach.  
   • Identify which steps or data structures need tweaking under the new lens.  
   • For example, if they want you to optimize for a different metric (memory vs. speed), call that out.

5. Narrate Your Adaptation  
   • Say out loud: “Okay, originally I was tracking frequency in a hash map and then scanning keys in sorted order. Under this new requirement to process streaming data, I’ll switch to a min-heap + window pointer.”  
   • Explaining your thought process demonstrates you’re flexible and thoughtful, not just mechanically coding.

6. Validate Complexity and Edge Cases  
   • Quickly run through: “With this change, our time complexity goes from O(n log n) to O(n), memory from O(n) to O(k). That still meets the target bounds, right?”  
   • Confirming complexity shows you haven’t lost sight of big-O even as you pivot.

7. Dive Back into Coding  
   • With clarifications in hand and a revised plan, start implementing the updated solution.  
   • Continue narrating (“Here’s where I initialize the data structure…”, “Now I’ll loop through each element and adjust my window…”) so the interviewer sees you staying on track.

By systematically pausing, paraphrasing, questioning, adapting, and re-validating, you’ll transform that curve ball into an opportunity to showcase your communication, flexibility, and analytical skills—exactly what interviewers want to see.

• He’s completely smitten—he regrets not recognizing her worth earlier.

   – Casts his love in religious terms: he speaks of devotion, reverence, even a kind of penance for not appreciating her earlier.  
   – Elevates her from mere romantic interest to an almost sacred object of adoration.

Here’s how to drop in “dummy” English text (coherent filler) anywhere in Word without copy-pasting:

Method 1 – The =rand() shortcut  
1. Click where you want your filler text.  
2. Type one of these and press Enter:  
   • =rand() – inserts the default three paragraphs of help-text.  
   • =rand(p, s) – p = number of paragraphs, s = sentences per paragraph.  
     Example: =rand(4,2)  
3. Word instantly replaces that line with your random text.

Method 2 – Insert a Rand field via the Ribbon  
1. Position the cursor where you want the text.  
2. Go to Insert → Quick Parts (or Text → Quick Parts) → Field…  
3. In the Field dialog:  
   – Under “Field names” choose “Rand.”  
   – In “Field options” enter the number of paragraphs and sentences.  
4. Click OK and Word will generate your filler text.

Method 3 – Manual field code  
1. Press Ctrl+F9 to insert a pair of field braces: { }  
2. Between them type: RAND p s  
   e.g. { RAND 3 5 }  
3. With the cursor inside the braces press F9 to update the field.  
4. Word replaces the field with p paragraphs of s sentences of random text.

Bonus:  
– If you’d rather have Latin “Lorem ipsum” filler, swap the field name: =lorem(p,s) instead of =rand.  
– If you want the old pangram (“The quick brown fox…”), use =rand.old(p,s).

instruction: Recommend some helpful activities or conversation starters to use at meetups to break the ice.

output:
Here are a handful of low-pressure activities and conversation prompts you can try at your next meetup to help people loosen up and start talking:

Activities  
1. Two Truths and a Lie  
   • Each person shares three statements about themselves—two true, one false.  
   • The group guesses which one’s the lie.  

2. Common-Ground Bingo  
   • Create a bingo card with traits or experiences (e.g., “Has traveled to Asia,” “Plays a musical instrument,” “Loves spicy food”).  
   • Participants mingle to find someone who matches each square.  

3. Speed Networking  
   • Break into pairs for 2–3 minute “mini-conversations.”  
   • After time’s up, rotate so everyone meets someone new.  

4. Would You Rather…?  
   • Ask fun, light-hearted dilemmas (“Would you rather have the ability to fly or be invisible?”).  
   • Everyone explains their choice.  

5. Human Knot  
   • Stand in a circle, reach across to grab two different people’s hands, then work together to untangle without letting go.  

6. Show & Tell  
   • Invite everyone to bring one small item that represents a hobby, passion, or recent achievement.  
   • Take turns explaining why it’s meaningful.  

7. Story Circle (One-Word at a Time)  
   • Sit in a circle. One person starts a story with a single word, the next person adds another word, and so on—see where the narrative goes!  

8. Photo Prompt  
   • Provide a random photo or postcard to each small group.  
   • Ask them to invent a backstory or caption for the image.  

9. Question Ball  
   • Write icebreaker questions on a beach ball.  
   • Toss the ball around; whoever catches it answers the question under their right thumb.  

10. Group Playlist  
   • Have everyone name one song they love.  
   • Compile into a shared playlist to spark conversation about musical tastes.  

Conversation Starters  
1. “What’s one thing you’ve learned in the last month that surprised you?”  
2. “If you could instantly become an expert in any skill, what would it be?”  
3. “What’s your go-to way to unwind after a busy day?”  
4. “Have you read or watched anything recently that you’d recommend?”  
5. “What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?”  
6. “If you could host a dinner party with any three people—living or dead—who would they be?”  
7. “What’s one place on your travel bucket list, and why?”  
8. “Which fictional character do you relate to most?”  
9. “What’s a hobby you’ve always wanted to try but haven’t yet?”  
10. “What’s the weirdest or funniest thing that’s happened to you this year?”  

Mix and match based on group size, energy level, and interests. The key is to keep it light, encourage everyone to participate, and follow up on any interesting tidbits people share. Good luck breaking the ice!

   • Notice and name 4 things you can touch (e.g. your shirt, the floor).  
   • Listen and name 3 things you can hear.  
   • Notice 2 things you can smell (or two favorite smells you can imagine).  
   • Become aware of 1 thing you can taste (or imagine a pleasant taste).  
   How it helps: Shifts your attention away from worrisome thoughts by anchoring you in the present moment and engaging your senses.  

2. Breathe (4-7-8 Pattern)  
   • Inhale gently through your nose for a mental count of 4.  
   • Hold that breath for a count of 7.  
   • Exhale slowly through your mouth for a count of 8.  
   • Repeat this cycle 3–5 times.  
   How it helps: Activates the parasympathetic (“rest and digest”) nervous system, slowing heart rate and reducing the physiological arousal that fuels anxiety.  

3. Visualize (Stress as an Object)  
   • Close your eyes and imagine your anxiety or stress as a physical object—perhaps a heavy rock, a knot of rope, or a dark cloud.  
   • Picture yourself holding it at arm’s length or setting it down on the floor.  
   • Mentally shrink it, dissolve it in light, or watch it float away.  
   How it helps: Externalizing anxiety turns vague, overwhelming feelings into something you can observe and manipulate, which fosters a sense of control and distance from the emotion.  

4. Reframe (Positive Affirmation or Question)  
   • Once you’ve “released” the object, ask yourself a gentle question such as “What do I need right now?” or “What small step can I take next?”  
   • Alternatively, repeat a short affirmation:  
     – “I am safe in this moment.”  
     – “I can handle what comes.”  
     – “One step at a time.”  
   How it helps: Redirects your mind from automatic negative thoughts toward problem-solving or self-compassion, reinforcing a more balanced, manageable perspective.  

Putting it all together takes only a few minutes. By alternating between sensory grounding, breath control, mental imagery, and cognitive reframing, you interrupt the anxiety cycle at multiple levels—physiological, emotional, and cognitive—and create space for calm and clarity.

Paper: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.
Explain: The dominant sequence transduction models

Here is a minimal working example using the popular “chessboard” package (which can read FEN strings directly) to typeset any position.  Just replace the value of the `setfen` option with your own FEN.

```latex
\documentclass[border=5pt]{standalone}
% the standalone class is optional; it just makes a tight PDF of the board
\usepackage{chessboard}    % main package for drawing boards
\usepackage{skak}          % provides move‐generator, fen parsing, etc.

\begin{document}

% Replace the FEN below by any position you like:
\chessboard[
  setfen=rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNBQKBNR b KQkq - 0 1,
  % turn off coordinates if you want a plain board:
  label=false,
  % you can also customize colors, highlighting, etc.
]

\end{document}
```

Explanation of the key points:

• We load  
  – `chessboard` for drawing the board and pieces,  
  – `skak` to make sure FEN parsing is available.  

• The command  
  `\chessboard[setfen=<FEN-string>]`  
  reads your FEN and draws the corresponding position.  

• You can further tweak the look with options like `label=false` (to hide the a–h/1–8 coordinates), color options, arrows, square highlights, etc.

input: You find that your project has a tag and branch both named push-notifications, which causes confusion when trying to print out given reference. How can you specify which branch you want to look at?
instruction: You will be asked to answer the following question as part of the LinkedIn Skill assessments.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text an answer to the question in the given input?
output:
When you have a tag and a branch with the same name, Git will by default resolve the shorter “namespace” first (tags live in refs/tags/ so “push-notifications” will pick the tag). To force Git to pick the branch, use its full ref name:

  git show refs/heads/push-notifications

Similarly, if you ever wanted the tag explicitly you could do:

  git show refs/tags/push-notifications

(And you can use refs/heads/... anywhere Git expects a rev – e.g. in git log, git diff, git rev-parse, git checkout, etc.)

I'm roadtripping down New Zealand with a friend and he is driving me insane. He hasn't enjoyed all the tours we've been on and doesn't want to chat about ANYTHING. We're a week into our trip and this is the quietest I've ever been when hanging out with another person as he rebuffs all my attempts at conversation. He wears his airpods in the car and around the accommodation - not that I've kept trying to talk to him. Honestly, he is bringing some seriously bad vibes to everything and it's ruining my trip.
We don't have anything booked in yet for the South Island, so I'm planning to ditch him in Wellington at the ferry. Probably book my own car in Picton and just relax alone for the rest of the trip. (Just thinking about it is such sharp relief that it makes me feel emotional. I'll pay whatever price I have to just to get away from him.)
Obviously telling him he is ruining my trip with his negative energy isn't the best way to approach this.
Any advice for the best approach so we can split amicably? Or at least not have an argument that ends with very hurt feelings?

Here’s a step-by-step way to pull this off as calmly and cleanly as possible:

1. Pick the right moment  
   • Find a quiet time when you’re both relaxed (over dinner or a coffee rather than mid-drive).  
   • Don’t ambush him in the car or on the ferry dock; give him a few minutes’ notice that you want to chat.

2. Use “I”-language, not “you”-accusations  
   • “I’ve realized I really need some solo time to recharge and enjoy the South Island at my own pace.”  
   • “I’m feeling stressed because my idea of this trip was a lot more talking, exploring and planning together—and I’m guessing you’ve been feeling the opposite.”

3. State what you want, not what’s wrong with him  
   • “So here’s what I’m thinking: I’m going to catch the ferry from Wellington on Wednesday at noon and book my own car in Picton. I’m hoping to spend the next week doing things at my own rhythm.”  
   • “If you’d rather keep going together, I totally understand—just let me know before I lock in my ferry & car.”

4. Offer flexibility and goodwill  
   • “I can help you re-arrange your spot on the ferry if you’d rather go that route.”  
   • “No hard feelings either way. I value our friendship, so I really want to keep things cool between us.”

5. Set clear logistics  
   • “I’m going to book the 12 pm ferry on Wednesday; if you want to switch to an earlier or later one, let me know by tomorrow.”  
   • “I’ll email you my car rental confirmation once it’s booked so you know I’m all set.”

6. End on a positive note  
   • “I appreciate you being open about how you want to travel, and I’m sorry things haven’t felt great this week.”  
   • “Let’s grab one more dinner in Wellington before I head off—my treat.”

By  
• Focusing on your needs (solo time)  
• Offering a simple plan/timeline  
• Showing you still care about the friendship  
you drastically reduce the risk of a blow-up. Good luck, and enjoy the rest of your trip!

Peter Weir’s Dead Poets Society, shot by Oscar–winning cinematographer John Seale, uses light and composition to reinforce the film’s themes of conformity and individual expression. Early boarding–school scenes employ cool, muted tones and soft, diffuse daylight through dorm-room windows, suggesting the stifling uniformity of Welton Academy. In contrast, moments of inspiration—like the boys discovering poetry in the cave—are lit with warmer, more direct sunlight, underlining Oliver’s emotional awakening.

Camera movement alternates between restrained, measured tracking shots in formal settings and more fluid handheld or crane moves during scenes of rebellion. In Professor Keating’s classroom, the camera often drifts in closer or tilts upward as he challenges his students, visually echoing his encouragement to “look at things from different angles.” Wide shots of the manicured lawns and austere buildings underscore the institution’s rigid order, while sudden close-ups on Robin Williams’s face capture the energy and vulnerability of his teaching style.

Seale’s framing also uses negative space and symmetry to highlight tension between the collective and the individual. Group tableaux—students lined up in perfect rows—contrast sharply with solitary figures standing apart when they dare to “seize the day.” This careful interplay of light, movement, and composition makes the cinematography a silent storyteller, reinforcing the film’s emotional stakes without ever overpowering the performances.

The ideal windows for visiting Sydney are late spring (September–November) or early autumn (March–May). Here’s why:  
1. Pleasant weather  
   • Temperatures generally range from 18–25 °C (64–77 °F), perfect for sightseeing, beach days and harbor cruises without the intense heat of mid-summer.  
2. Fewer crowds  
   • You’ll avoid the peak-season rush of international tourists and school holidays, meaning shorter lines at attractions like the Opera House and Taronga Zoo.  
3. Better travel deals  
   • Airfares and accommodation rates tend to dip just outside the December–January high season, so you can often secure more competitive prices.  
4. Outdoor events and festivals  
   • Spring brings the Sculptures by the Sea coastal exhibition and wildflower blooms in the Royal Botanic Garden. Early autumn offers the Sydney Writers’ Festival and a milder Vivid Sydney schedule before the winter chill.  
5. Whale-watching opportunities  
   • Humpback whales migrate past Sydney’s coast from late May through early November, so spring visits give you a good chance of spotting them on a cruise or from coastal lookouts.

input: Zinc is an essential mineral that is required for good health. It is involved in many biochemical processes in the body and is necessary for the proper functioning of the immune system. Excess zink is not harmful as it is excreted in the urine.
instruction: The given article should be checked for any scientific errors and corrected if necessary.

output:
Corrected version:

Zinc is an essential trace mineral required for normal growth, development and numerous biochemical processes in the body. It plays critical roles in DNA and protein synthesis, enzyme function, wound healing, taste perception and especially in the proper functioning of the immune system.  

Because the body does not have a large zinc storage depot, regular dietary intake is necessary. Zinc is absorbed primarily in the small intestine. Unused zinc is eliminated mainly in the feces (with smaller amounts lost in urine and sweat).  

While zinc deficiency impairs immune function, wound repair and growth, excessive zinc intake can be harmful. Chronic high zinc consumption (above the tolerable upper intake level of about 40 mg per day for adults) may cause gastrointestinal upset, interfere with copper and iron absorption (leading to anemia and impaired immunity), reduce “good” HDL cholesterol levels and, in severe cases, produce neurological symptoms.  

Recommended dietary allowances vary by age, sex and life stage, but a balanced diet containing meat, seafood, dairy or fortified cereals generally provides adequate zinc without risk of toxicity.

Dear Sarah,

I can’t tell you how proud Dad and I are as we watch you pack your bags for college. This new chapter will be filled with excitement, challenges, and incredible opportunities to learn about yourself and the world around you. Before you head out, I wanted to share a few thoughts on staying grounded, making connections, and keeping our family bond strong.

First, remember that relationships take effort. Call or video‐chat a couple of times each week—no need to wait for something big to happen. We love hearing about your day‐to‐day adventures, and it will help you feel supported when classes get tough. If you find yourself overwhelmed, pick up the phone; sometimes a brief chat or even a text exchange can lift your spirits.

Second, be open to meeting new people. Say yes to study groups, club events, or dorm gatherings. Introduce yourself with a simple smile and “Hi, I’m Sarah.” You don’t have to become best friends right away—start small: share notes, grab coffee, or ask about someone’s major. You’ll be surprised how quickly those small connections bloom into genuine friendships.

Finally, don’t forget to carve out “family time.” Maybe it’s a monthly group video dinner or a shared playlist of songs we love. We’ll be cheering you on with every exam you pass and every milestone you reach. Your room might be empty now, but our hearts are always with you.

We believe in you, we’re proud of you, and we can’t wait to see the person you become. Go chase your dreams—and know there’s always a home waiting for you here.

Mom and Dad

Color Palette (4 colors only)  
• Emerald Green: foliage of both tree species, undergrowth, and lower mountain slopes  
• Cobalt Blue: sky and reflections in the water  
• Golden Ochre: sunlit grass, earth path, and fallen leaves  
• Titanium White: birch bark, water highlights (foam, ripples), and mountain snowcaps  

1. Foreground  
- Elements:  
  • A sturdy oak tree at left, its broad canopy rendered in swirling impasto strokes of emerald green. The thick, curved brushwork mimics the oak’s gnarled bark and dense leaf clusters.  
  • A slender grove of birch saplings to the right, their smooth trunks lightly sketched in titanium white with a palette knife, creating raised ridges that catch light. Their delicate leaves are dabbed in golden ochre.  
  • A narrow earthen path winds between the trees, painted in broad, horizontal sweeps of golden ochre, with occasional flecks of emerald green to suggest tufts of grass.  

- Textures & Brushwork:  
  • Oak foliage: heavy, circular dabs of paint (impasto) to evoke thickness and shadow.  
  • Birch bark: thin, vertical palette-knife strokes in white for crisp texture.  
  • Path: flat, smooth underpainting of ochre, finished with soft brushing to show compacted earth.  

2. Middle Ground  
- Elements:  
  • A tranquil pond reflecting the cobalt-blue sky. The surface is rendered with long, horizontal brushstrokes that blend blue and white at the edges, suggesting gentle ripples and sunlit sparkles.  
  • A small cluster of pine trees on the far bank, their triangular forms built from quick, stippled touches of emerald green, with white highlights on wind-whipped needles.  

- Textures & Brushwork:  
  • Water: silky, glazed layers of cobalt blue topped by thin white highlights applied with the tip of a flat brush.  
  • Pine needles: pointed, upward flicks of the brush in green and white, giving a spiky, dynamic feel.  

3. Background  
- Elements:  
  • A distant mountain range rising under the sky. The foothills bear a light wash of emerald green and golden ochre—applied thinly—melding into misty slopes.  
  • The peaks are capped with thick swaths of titanium white, forming crisp, snowy ridges against the sky.  
  • Above it all, a clear cobalt-blue sky occupies the uppermost third of the canvas.  

- Textures & Brushwork:  
  • Lower slopes: soft, blended glazes of green and ochre, laid on with a large soft brush to suggest atmospheric perspective.  
  • Snowcaps: bold, chiseled strokes of white with a palette knife, giving a sharper contrast and sense of rocky edge.  
  • Sky: smooth, nearly seamless gradation of cobalt blue achieved by gentle horizontal sweeps and a lightly dampened brush.  

Overall Harmony  
By restricting the palette to four colors and assigning each exclusively to certain elements, the painting achieves a cohesive, tranquil atmosphere. Varied brush techniques—impasto for weight, glazing for distance, stippling for foliage, and palette-knife texturing for bark and snow—distinguish each layer while unifying them in a balanced composition.

Dramatis Personae  
Dr. Lina Chen – Quantum physicist, head of Project ChronoGate.  
Major Alex Rivera – Military liaison to the time-travel project.  
Envoy Ka’Tal – Aureonian diplomat and xenobiologist.  
General Serin Vox – Commander of Aureon’s planetary defense forces.  
Adrian Blake – ChronoGate technician and pilot.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  

ACT I: EARTH (Aurora City, Project ChronoGate Facility – 2147 A.D.)  
One stark laboratory, humming time-field generators at its core.

Scene 1  

(Blue light bathes a central console. DR. LINA CHEN adjusts a crystal matrix. MAJOR ALEX RIVERA stands rigid, arms folded.)

DR. LINA CHEN:  
Projected invasion window: forty-eight hours. The Xerathi rifts will open in low Earth orbit, pouring in bio-drones. We have one chance to call for aid.  

MAJOR ALEX RIVERA:  
You really think Aureon even exists? This “ChronoGate” is untested on living subjects.  

DR. LINA CHEN (softly):  
Our only hope. Time travel and interstellar jump—rolled into one. If we don’t send someone through now, Earth falls.  

(Major Rivera’s comm unit crackles.)

RADIO VOICE (voice-over):  
Final diagnostics green. Gate stabilizer at 97 percent. Countdown on your mark.  

MAJOR ALEX RIVERA (looking at Dr. Chen):  
All right. We go. You and I. Everyone else is staying here.  

DR. LINA CHEN (nodding):  
I’ll open the link to Aureon. You keep an eye out for any temporal backlash.  

(They step onto the transparent platform. The room hums louder. A strobing wormhole opens. They exchange a breathless glance.)

DR. LINA CHEN (over roar):  
See you on the other side.  

(They vanish into pale light. Blackout.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  

ACT II: PLANET AUREON (Capital Thr-Var – 3123 FUTURE AUREONIAN STANDARD)  
A vast council chamber of polished iridescent stone. A fractured time-gate hovers mid-air.

Scene 1  

(Envoy KA’TAL stands before the damaged gate. GENERAL SERIN VOX stands at her side. DR. LINA CHEN and MAJOR RIVERA stumble through, disoriented. ADRIAN BLAKE’s voice crackles from a floating comm-orb.)

ADRIAN BLAKE (voice-over):  
Status: Gate integrity holding at eighty-three percent. Lina, confirm your position.  

DR. LINA CHEN (touching alien glyphs):  
We’re on Aureon. The date stamp reads 3123 A.S.T. That’s eleven hundred years your future.  

GENERAL SERIN VOX (arms crossed):  
You speak of aliens called Xerathi in Earth orbit? Why should Aureon care?  

MAJOR ALEX RIVERA:  
They conquered your worlds a millennium ago. They enslaved your people for centuries—until you fought them off with chronotech. Now they’re coming for Earth.  

ENVoy KA’TAL (to Serin):  
He’s right. We barely sealed the last Xerathi tear in our sky. They wait for a weakness.  

GENERAL SERIN VOX (scowling):  
Our resources are low. We cannot divert fleets across time and space on rumor.  

DR. LINA CHEN (urgent):  
We have your gate controls. With our calibration, we can bring your ships to Earth—if you trust us.  

ADRIAN BLAKE (voice-over, browning tone):  
ChronoGate is destabilizing. The temporal flux is spiking. If we maintain the link too long, it will collapse in a rupture that could swallow this entire planet.  

GENERAL SERIN VOX (shocked):  
Then we have minutes, not hours.  

KA’TAL (placing a hand on Serin’s arm):  
We cannot abandon our kin—even if it costs Aureon itself.  

GENERAL SERIN VOX (after a beat):  
Very well. We commit our last carrier squadron.  

ADRIAN BLAKE (voice-over):  
Countdown to jump in ten… nine… eight…  

DR. LINA CHEN (her hand on Adrian’s orb):  
Adrian, once they arrive on Earth, can you shut down the gate safely?  

ADRIAN BLAKE (quietly):  
It takes one person inside to collapse the core. Outside, we lose control.  

DR. LINA CHEN:  
We’ll be ready.  

(The chamber glows. Aureonian ships materialize around the gate’s rim.)

GENERAL SERIN VOX (raising his voice):  
To Earth, then! For the future of two worlds!  

(He and the Aureonian pilots step through. The gate’s light flickers. KA’TAL holds Dr. Chen’s hand.)

KA’TAL:  
May fate be kinder than time.  

(Blackout.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  

ACT III: EARTH (Aurora City Defense Plaza – 2147 A.D., hours later)  
Ruined skyline. A battered time-gate stands crumbling at center stage. Aureonian fighters swarm overhead; Xerathi warships loom.

Scene 1  

(Dr. Lina Chen and Major Rivera crouch behind shattered concrete. ADRIAN BLAKE steps from the gate’s core chamber, face illuminated by sparking conduits.)

ADRIAN BLAKE:  
The reactor’s meltdown in sixty seconds. If I don’t vent it from inside, the gate tears a hole through time—and drags us all in.  

MAJOR ALEX RIVERA (rushing to him):  
There’s got to be another way! We can collapse it remotely.  

ADRIAN BLAKE (shaking his head):  
Only manual trip. One person.  

DR. LINA CHEN (voice breaking):  
Adrian—you’re the only one who can navigate the time-flux pathway.  

ADRIAN BLAKE (smiles sadly):  
Then I’ll see you on the other side… I guess.  

KA’TAL (appearing through a side ramp, holographic link active):  
Lina! We’re holding the Xerathi back in orbit. The gate’s your only edge.  

DR. LINA CHEN (to Ka’Tal):  
Thank you. Keep fighting.  

(Adrian slips inside the core chamber as sparks shower the platform.)  

ADRIAN BLAKE (yelling):  
Now, Lina—flip the primary switch!  

(Dr. Chen slams a lever. A shockwave of pale light surges, sweeping across the stage. The Xerathi rifts collapse overhead with violent roars. The Aureonian ships disengage and leap away. The gate implodes in a silent flash. Silence.)

Scene 2 (Epilogue)  

(The rubble is gone. A memorial plaque: “In Memory of Adrian Blake—He Shattered Time to Save Us All.” DR. LINA CHEN stands before it, flanked by MAJOR RIVERA and ENVoy KA’TAL. A distant Aureonian cruiser glimmers in the sky.)

DR. LINA CHEN (softly):  
He gave us the future we dared only imagine. Time travel used for mercy, not conquest.  

MAJOR ALEX RIVERA:  
Earth owes him—and Aureon—everything.  

ENVoy KA’TAL:  
May our worlds forever stand side by side, in all times.  

(They place flowers. Light fades on three figures united beneath a shared dawn.)

Curtain.

Please ensure that the meditation does not incorporate any religious or spiritual elements. Additionally, provide guidance on the ideal time and duration for each part of the meditation.

Below is a simple, secular 10-minute guided meditation for stress relief. First you’ll find a quick overview of each part with its ideal duration. After that, you’ll see the full spoken script you can read or record. Feel free to adjust the pacing slightly to match your own voice or group.

—–––— Meditation Outline —–––—

Part 1: Settle and Prepare  
• Duration: 1 minute  
• Goal: Find comfort, establish posture, brief centering

Part 2: Gentle Breath Awareness  
• Duration: 2 minutes  
• Goal: Notice the natural rhythm of your breathing

Part 3: Deep Breathing Practice  
• Duration: 2 minutes  
• Goal: Use a simple count to encourage fuller, calming breaths

Part 4: Body Scan for Release  
• Duration: 3 minutes  
• Goal: Systematically relax major muscle groups

Part 5: Closing and Transition  
• Duration: 2 minutes  
• Goal: Re-ground, carry calm forward

—–––— Full Guided Script —–––—

Part 1: Settle and Prepare (1 minute)  
Begin by finding a comfortable position—seated on a chair or cushion, or lying down if you prefer.  
Gently close your eyes or soften your gaze toward the floor.  
Let your hands rest easily in your lap or by your sides.  
Allow your spine to be natural and upright, shoulders soft, jaw unclenched.  
Take three easy, full inhales and exhales just to arrive fully in this moment.  
With each out-breath, feel your body settling a little more.  

Part 2: Gentle Breath Awareness (2 minutes)  
Now, simply notice your breath as it flows in and out.  
There is no need to change it—just observe the coolness at your nostrils, the slight rise of your chest or belly, the warmth as you exhale.  
If your mind drifts, that’s okay—gently bring your attention back to the sensation of breathing.  
For the next two minutes, let your awareness rest softly on each inhale and each exhale.  

(Allow roughly 2 minutes of quiet here.)  

Part 3: Deep Breathing Practice (2 minutes)  
Next, we’ll deepen the breath.  
Inhale slowly for a count of four—1…2…3…4—feeling your belly expand.  
Pause for a brief moment.  
Then exhale gently for a count of six—1…2…3…4…5…6—letting go of any tension.  
Again: inhale 1–2–3–4… hold… exhale 1–2–3–4–5–6.  
Continue this pattern, feeling each breath nourish and release.  

(Allow roughly 2 minutes of this breathing pattern.)  

Part 4: Body Scan for Release (3 minutes)  
Now bring your attention to your feet. Notice any sensations—warmth, pressure, tension. With each out-breath, imagine your feet softening.  
Shift up to your lower legs and knees. Inhale calm into the area, exhale and let go.  
Move your awareness to your thighs and hips. Pause, breathe in, and on the out-breath release any stiffness.  
Continue up into your abdomen and chest. Notice how your torso expands and contracts. On each exhale, soften through the core.  
Bring your focus to your shoulders—breathe into any tight spots, then let them drop.  
Scan down each arm to your hands and fingertips, releasing gently.  
Lastly, shift to your neck, jaw, and face. With each out-breath, allow these areas to become smooth and relaxed.  

(Spend about 15–20 seconds on each region, moving at a calm, unhurried pace.)  

Part 5: Closing and Transition (2 minutes)  
Return your awareness now to your overall breath—natural, easy, steady.  
Notice the sense of space and ease you’ve created.  
Take three final, nourishing breaths together:  
Inhale calm… exhale tension.  
Inhale clarity… exhale any lingering stress.  
Inhale presence… exhale the rest of your breath.  
When you’re ready, gently wiggle fingers and toes, stretch your arms or legs if you wish, and softly open your eyes or lift your gaze.  
Carry this feeling of calm with you as you move into the rest of your day.  

— End of Meditation —  

Total time: approximately 10 minutes.  
Feel free to practice daily or whenever you need to reset.

instruction: Describe the properties of water without using adjectives.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text a description of water?
Is the generated text free from the use of any adjectives to describe the water?
output:
Properties of water

1. Composition and structure at scale of molecules  
- A water molecule contains hydrogen nuclei and an oxygen nucleus.  
- The sharing of electrons bonds these nuclei within the molecule.

2. Charge distribution and attraction between molecules  
- Separation of protons and electrons at atom sites yields regions with a surplus of protons and regions with a surplus of electrons.  
- Regions carrying a surplus of protons attract regions carrying a surplus of electrons across molecules via charge interactions.  
- These attractions form hydrogen bonds between molecules.

3. Phase behavior at one atmosphere pressure  
- At or below freezing point, input of heat fails to break all hydrogen bonds, and molecules stay linked, producing water in a form that resists change of shape.  
- Between freezing point and boiling point, input of heat breaks some hydrogen bonds while allowing molecules to remain in contact; this yields water that conforms to container shape.  
- At or above boiling point, input of heat overcomes bond formation, and molecules move far apart, producing water vapor.

4. Volume change upon freezing  
- When heat removal drives water from a form where bonds break and allow sliding to a form where bonds hold molecules in an arrangement, the space that water molecules occupy increases; thus, the form where bonds hold molecules floats on the form where bonds allow sliding under those conditions.

5. Thermal energy effects  
- Energy input breaks hydrogen bonds, driving phase changes from solid to liquid and from liquid to gas.  
- Energy release occurs when hydrogen bonds form, driving phase changes from gas to liquid and from liquid to solid.

6. Solvent capability  
- Water dissolves substances that dissociate into ions, enabling movement of charge carriers.

7. Proton transfer in reactions  
- Water donates and accepts protons in chemical reactions, facilitating proton exchange between species.

8. Transport medium  
- Water acts as a medium for transport of molecules and ions.

output:
1. Crust  
The drilling rig’s drill bit bit into the granite crust like a hungry shark tearing through flesh. Above, the sun glinted off the platform’s steel supports as the crew monitored vibrations on their screens. Beneath us, the brittle crust shivered, then gave way to a strange, luminous glow as we descended. The rocks shifted from familiar granite to basalt, and we felt the first real tremors of crossing from Earth’s solid outer skin into something far denser.

2. Upper Mantle  
When the crust finally slipped into the past, we entered the upper mantle—a realm of viscous rock heated to over a thousand degrees Celsius. Our vehicle’s exterior panels glowed red from the relentless heat but held firm. The ground beneath us roiled in slow, convulsive motions, like a pond about to boil. Mineral crystals elongated and realigned under crushing pressure, creating bands of strange, swirling obsidian fields that pressed against our windows.

3. Transition Zone  
Pressures rose to unimaginable levels as we plunged deeper, and the environment shifted abruptly. We encountered the transition zone, where the composition of minerals changed—olivine morphed into wadsleyite, then ringwoodite. It felt as if we were traveling through a geologist’s kaleidoscope. Our instruments shook with each metamorphosis, but the narrow window in the cabin offered a breathtaking spectacle of crystallization waves pulsing around us.

4. Lower Mantle  
Beyond the transition zone lay the lower mantle, a region of nearly incompressible rock with pressures millions of times greater than atmospheric. Here, the temperature soared toward 3,000°C, and seismic waves raced through the dense iron-magnesium silicates. The rock glowed faintly orange, and we slipped through it like a ship sailing a molten sea. Every jolt reminded us how close we were to the planet’s beating heart.

5. Outer Core  
Suddenly, the rocky confines vanished, and we plunged into the outer core—a fluid ocean of liquid iron and nickel. Magnetic eddies swirled around our craft, tugging at its metallic hull. We felt the pull of Earth’s magnetic field grow stronger, buffeting us with invisible currents. Flames of molten metal writhed in mesmerizing currents outside our windows, reminding us that our planet’s magnetic shield was born here in this roiling inferno.

6. Inner Core  
At last, we breached the boundary into the inner core, a solid iron sphere under pressures exceeding 3.5 million atmospheres. The heat peaked above 5,000°C, but the unyielding iron lattice held firm against the squeeze. Here, time seemed to stand still. We hovered in total silence, surrounded by a metallic glow so intense it felt like staring into the sun’s core. In that moment, we understood the true heart of our world: a glowing, unbreakable engine powering every rock, river, and breath above.

30-Minute Full-Body Routine (No Equipment Required)

Warm-Up (5 minutes)  
• Arm circles, leg swings, hip openers, light jogging or high-knees in place.

Main Circuit (20 minutes)  
Perform each exercise in order, resting 30–45 seconds between exercises. After you complete all five (or six) moves, rest 1 minute and repeat the circuit. Aim for 2–3 total circuits depending on pace.

1. Push-Ups  
   • Sets × Reps: 3 × 12  
   • Primary Muscles: Pectoralis major (chest), anterior deltoids (front shoulders), triceps.

2. Bodyweight Squats  
   • Sets × Reps: 3 × 15  
   • Primary Muscles: Quadriceps, gluteus maximus (butt), hamstrings.

3. Bent-Over Rows (with dumbbells, resistance band, or filled water jugs)  
   • Sets × Reps: 3 × 12  
   • Primary Muscles: Latissimus dorsi and rhomboids (upper/mid back), posterior deltoids, biceps.

4. Dumbbell (or Band) Shoulder Press  
   • Sets × Reps: 3 × 10  
   • Primary Muscles: Deltoids (shoulders), trapezius (upper back), triceps, upper chest.

5. Forward Lunges  
   • Sets × Reps: 3 × 10 each leg  
   • Primary Muscles: Quadriceps, gluteus maximus, hamstrings, calves for stability.

6. Front Plank  
   • Sets × Duration: 3 × 45–60 seconds  
   • Primary Muscles: Rectus abdominis and transverse abdominis (abs), obliques (side core), erector spinae (lower back).

Cool-Down (5 minutes)  
• Static stretches for chest, quads, hamstrings, shoulders and hip flexors.  
• Focus on deep breathing and slowly lowering your heart rate.

Time Breakdown  
• Warm-Up: 5 min  
• Circuit: ~20 min (6 exercises × 3 sets = 18 sets; ≈40–50 seconds per set + rest)  
• Cool-Down: 5 min  

Adjust rest periods or number of circuits to fit exactly 30 minutes. This routine hits all major muscle groups—chest, legs, back, shoulders and core—while keeping the pace high for an efficient, full-body workout.

INDIVIDUALIZED EDUCATION PLAN (IEP) OUTLINE  
Duration: 12 months  
Student Profile (example fields)  
• Name, grade, date of birth  
• Primary disability: dyslexia  
• Strengths and interests  
• Present levels of academic performance (reading accuracy, fluency, comprehension, writing, spelling)

I. Annual Goals and Objectives  
• By the end of 12 months, student will read grade-level text with 90% accuracy and 120 words per minute in repeated readings.  
• Student will decode multisyllabic words using learned syllable-division rules with 85% accuracy.  
• Student will increase reading comprehension to 80% accuracy on literal and inferential questions.  
• Student will produce a five-paragraph expository essay with appropriate organization, mechanics, and use of vocabulary.  
• Student will self-advocate for accommodations in mainstream classrooms with teacher support.

II. Monthly Learning Goals  
Month 1  
  – Conduct baseline assessments (phonemic awareness, decoding, fluency, comprehension)  
  – Introduce structured, multisensory phonics program (e.g., Orton-Gillingham approach)  
  – Goal: identify and manipulate phonemes in spoken words with 90% accuracy  

Month 2  
  – Teach letter–sound correspondences and blending strategies using manipulatives and tile boards  
  – Goal: decode CVC and CVCE words with 85% accuracy  

Month 3  
  – Introduce common irregular (high-frequency) sight words and orthographic patterns  
  – Goal: read and spell first-grade sight words with 90% mastery  

Month 4  
  – Focus on closed, open, silent-e, vowel team, and r-controlled syllable types  
  – Goal: correctly divide and decode two-syllable words with 80% accuracy  

Month 5  
  – Implement repeated reading fluency drills with short passages  
  – Goal: increase oral reading rate by 10 words per minute on monitored texts  

Month 6  
  – Explicit instruction in morphological units (prefixes, suffixes, root words)  
  – Goal: decode and define 20 new multisyllabic words using morphological analysis  

Month 7  
  – Build academic vocabulary through semantic mapping and context clue exercises  
  – Goal: correctly use and define 15 grade-appropriate vocabulary words in writing  

Month 8  
  – Teach comprehension strategies: predicting, questioning, clarifying, summarizing  
  – Goal: answer literal questions with 85% accuracy on instructional-level texts  

Month 9  
  – Advance to inferential and critical thinking questions; use graphic organizers (story maps, T-charts)  
  – Goal: respond to inferential questions with 75% accuracy  

Month 10  
  – Focus on sentence construction, grammar mechanics, and paragraph writing using step-by-step writing templates  
  – Goal: write a coherent paragraph with topic sentence, supporting details, and conclusion  

Month 11  
  – Teach essay planning: thesis development, topic outline, transitions, editing strategies  
  – Goal: produce a four- to five-paragraph essay with fewer than five mechanical errors  

Month 12  
  – Develop self-advocacy and study-skills plan: how to request accommodations, note-taking strategies, test-taking tips  
  – Goal: independently identify and request two appropriate accommodations in mainstream classes  

III. Specific Accommodations  
• Extended time on tests and assignments (time and a half or double time)  
• Daily small-group or 1:1 multisensory reading instruction  
• Use of colored overlays or reading strips to reduce visual stress  
• Preferential seating (front row or away from visual/auditory distractions)  
• Chunking assignments into smaller, manageable parts  
• Frequent breaks during long reading or testing tasks  
• Allowing oral responses or dictation in lieu of written work when appropriate  
• Use of graphic organizers for planning reading responses and written compositions  
• Provide teacher or peer-taped lectures and written outlines of lessons  
• Frequent progress monitoring and immediate corrective feedback  

IV. Potential Assistive Technology Resources  
• Text-to-Speech (TTS) software: NaturalReader, Kurzweil 3000, Read&Write by Texthelp  
• Speech-to-Text (dictation) tools: Dragon NaturallySpeaking, Google Voice Typing  
• Audiobook services: Learning Ally, Bookshare, Audible (with dyslexia settings)  
• Word prediction and grammar support: Co:Writer, Ghotit Real Writer  
• Specialized dyslexia-friendly fonts and overlays: OpenDyslexic font, Lexie Readable, colored screen filters  
• Electronic graphic organizer apps: Inspiration Maps, MindMeister, Popplet  
• Note-taking support: Livescribe Smartpen, Sonocent Audio Notetaker  
• Reading guides and trackers: IntelliTools Big Eye Reader, Reading Rulers  
• Mobile/tablet apps: Voice Dream Reader, SnapType, Dyslexia Quest  
• Organizational and scheduling apps: Google Calendar with reminders, Trello boards for assignment management

V. Progress Monitoring and Review  
• Bi-weekly data collection on fluency (WCPM) and accuracy  
• Monthly running records and comprehension probes  
• Quarterly writing samples evaluated with a rubric for mechanics and organization  
• Semi-annual IEP review meeting to adjust goals, accommodations, and technology as needed

End of Plan.

Vincent van Gogh’s Starry Night (1889) displays a masterful interplay of composition, color, and technique that conveys intense emotion and movement. The painting is organized around an undulating sky that dominates nearly three-quarters of the canvas. Swirling clouds, crescents, and orbs of light converge in rhythmic patterns, drawing the eye in continuous loops across the scene. Below, a tranquil village clusters around a bold, flame-shaped cypress tree that bridges earth and sky, reinforcing a dialogue between the terrestrial and the celestial.

Van Gogh’s color palette contrasts deep ultramarines and indigos with vibrant yellows and whites. The stars and moon glow against the dark backdrop, producing a dynamic push-pull effect. Thick impasto brushstrokes create texture and depth; each stroke appears to pulsate, heightening the sense of motion and emotional intensity. By layering paint in sinuous, expressive lines, van Gogh transforms a nocturnal landscape into a living, breathing vision.

Technically, Starry Night reflects van Gogh’s late style—he abandons precise realism in favor of a visceral, subjective approach. The composition and colors work together to evoke a sense of spiritual longing and turbulent energy, suggesting both hope and unrest. The cypress tree’s upward sweep seems to funnel earthly grief into cosmic light.

Significance and Impact: Starry Night stands as a landmark in Post-Impressionism, influencing generations of artists with its bold expressiveness. Its enduring power lies in van Gogh’s innovative fusion of technique, emotion, and symbolism, forever reshaping the language of modern art.

instruction: Using a Punnett square, predict the genotypic and phenotypic ratios of offspring produced by a cross between two individuals: one heterozygous for two Mendelian inheritance traits (AaBb) and the other homozygous dominant for one trait and heterozygous for the other (AABb). Please ensure to provide a clear explanation of the genotypic and phenotypic outcomes, including possible combinations and their respective ratios.
decomposed_questions: Does the generated text include a Punnett square?

Does the generated Punnett square accurately display the potential offspring genotypes resulting from the given cross?
Does the generated text provide a clear explanation of the genotypic outcomes resulting from this cross, including the various genotype combinations and their respective ratios?
Is the provided explanation and interpretation of the genotypic outcomes, including all possible genotype combinations and their respective ratios, accurate?
Does the generated text provide a clear explanation of the phenotypic outcomes resulting from this cross, including the various phenotype combinations and their respective ratios?
Is the provided explanation and interpretation of the phenotypic outcomes, including all possible phenotype combinations and their respective ratios, accurate?
output:
Here’s how you can work it out step by step without any fancy formatting—just lists and simple text.

1. Parent genotypes  
   – Parent 1: AaBb  
   – Parent 2: AABb  

2. List the gametes each parent can make  
   – From AaBb you get four gametes, each at ¼:  
     • AB  
     • Ab  
     • aB  
     • ab  
   – From AABb you get two gametes, each at ½:  
     • AB  
     • Ab  

3. Set up the Punnett‐square “matrix” (4 rows × 2 columns)  
   Rows = Parent 1 gametes; Columns = Parent 2 gametes  
   
     Columns →      AB        Ab  
     Rows ↓  
     AB        →   AABB      AABb  
     Ab        →   AABb      AAbb  
     aB        →   AaBB      AaBb  
     ab        →   AaBb      Aabb  
   
   Each cell has probability (¼ × ½) = 1/8.

4. Tally the genotypes (out of 8)  
   – AABB : 1  
   – AABb : 2  
   – AAbb : 1  
   – AaBB : 1  
   – AaBb : 2  
   – Aabb : 1  

   Genotypic ratio  
   AABB : AABb : AAbb : AaBB : AaBb : Aabb = 1 : 2 : 1 : 1 : 2 : 1  

5. Determine the phenotypes  
   Assume A is dominant to a, B is dominant to b.  
   – For the A‐trait: every offspring has at least one A (because Parent 2 is AA), so 100% show the dominant A phenotype.  
   – For the B‐trait: only bb individuals show the recessive phenotype. We have two bb genotypes (AAbb and Aabb), each 1/8, for a total of 2/8 = ¼. The other 6/8 = ¾ are B_ (dominant B).  

   Therefore the two‐trait phenotypic classes are:  
   – A_B_ (dominant A, dominant B): 6/8  
   – A_bb (dominant A, recessive b): 2/8  

   Phenotypic ratio A_B_ : A_bb = 6 : 2, which simplifies to 3 : 1 for the B‐trait (A is fixed dominant).  

Summary  
– Genotypic ratio (out of 8): 1 AABB : 2 AABb : 1 AAbb : 1 AaBB : 2 AaBb : 1 Aabb  
– Phenotypic ratio:  
   • 75% A (dominant) & B (dominant)  
   • 25% A (dominant) & bb (recessive)

instruction: Generate two matrices, A and B, where A is a 4x3 matrix and B is a 3x2 matrix, by randomly selecting numbers from the set {0, 1, 2}. Then, calculate the product C by multiplying A and B, denoted as C = A * B.

output:
Here is one possible random choice (all entries drawn from {0,1,2}) and the resulting product:

A (4×3) =  
[ [0, 2, 1],  
  [1, 0, 2],  
  [2, 1, 1],  
  [0, 0, 2] ]

B (3×2) =  
[ [1, 2],  
  [0, 1],  
  [2, 0] ]

Now compute C = A·B, which will be a 4×2 matrix. Entry (i,j) of C is the dot‐product of row i of A with column j of B:

1. Row 1 of A = [0,2,1]  
   • C₁₁ = 0·1 + 2·0 + 1·2 = 2  
   • C₁₂ = 0·2 + 2·1 + 1·0 = 2

2. Row 2 of A = [1,0,2]  
   • C₂₁ = 1·1 + 0·0 + 2·2 = 5  
   • C₂₂ = 1·2 + 0·1 + 2·0 = 2

3. Row 3 of A = [2,1,1]  
   • C₃₁ = 2·1 + 1·0 + 1·2 = 4  
   • C₃₂ = 2·2 + 1·1 + 1·0 = 5

4. Row 4 of A = [0,0,2]  
   • C₄₁ = 0·1 + 0·0 + 2·2 = 4  
   • C₄₂ = 0·2 + 0·1 + 2·0 = 0

Hence

C = A·B =  
[ [2, 2],  
  [5, 2],  
  [4, 5],  
  [4, 0] ]

output:
I bought these noise-canceling headphones hoping for an immersive, distraction-free listening experience, but after two weeks of daily use I’ve come away deeply disappointed. Here are my observations by category:

Sound Quality  
• Lack of clarity in vocals: At medium volume (around 60/100 on my phone) mids sounded muddy—voices blended into the instrumental instead of sitting forward in the mix. On podcasts I constantly found myself cranking the volume just to make out what was being said.  
• Overbearing bass, thin highs: The advertised “balanced signature” turned out to be more “boomy low end, tinny treble.” On tracks like “Billie Jean” the kick drum dominated, while cymbals and snare had no snap. Even my old budget earbuds delivered crisper highs.  
• Noticeable background hiss: With noise cancellation switched on but no music playing, I could hear a faint white noise. In a quiet room, that hiss was more distracting than the ambient sounds these headphones supposedly cancel.

Comfort  
• Clamping pressure: Right out of the box the clamping force felt excessive. After just 30 minutes of wear, I had discomfort around the temples and felt my head getting hot under the headband.  
• Rough ear pads: The synthetic leather feels stiff and plasticky rather than supple. After an hour or two the edges began digging in, and I even had red marks around my ears. I replaced them briefly with a third-party velour pad, which helped slightly—but at an extra cost.  
• Poor fit for glasses: I wear thin-rimmed glasses and these cups are shallow. The arms of my glasses press uncomfortably against my head, which defeats the purpose of “all-day comfort.”

Design  
• Flimsy hinges: The foldable mechanism uses thin plastic hinges that creak and feel like they could snap if handled roughly. On my fourth commute the left earcup hinge squeaked loudly every time I tilted it.  
• Mute and ANC buttons: The button layout is confusing. I often muted my calls by mistake when trying to toggle noise cancellation, and the raised ANC button offers almost no tactile feedback.  
• Cheap finish: The matte plastic picks up fingerprints and scratches easily. Within days I had visible scuffs along the sides. The slick look you see in marketing photos doesn’t hold up to real-world use.

Battery Life  
• Far below advertised: The manufacturer claims “up to 30 hours” of ANC-on playback. In my tests—streaming Spotify at 70% volume with noise cancellation engaged—I managed only about 18 hours before the low-battery warning.  
• Slow recharge: It takes nearly three full hours to go from zero to 100%. There’s no quick-charge option, so if you forget to plug them in overnight you’re stuck waiting.  
• Drain in standby: Even when power-off, the headphones drain a few percent each day. Leaving them unused for a weekend meant they were nearly dead by Monday morning.

Bottom Line  
Given my experience, I can’t recommend these headphones. The noise-cancellation is barely adequate, the sound signature feels unbalanced, and the physical comfort and build quality fall short of even mid-range competitors. If you value clear vocals, ergonomic padding, a solid hinge mechanism, or reliable battery life, you’ll be better off looking at alternatives like the Brand X QuietMaster or the SilentPro 700. These headphones simply didn’t deliver on the key promises that mattered most to me.

Strengths  
• Agility and Innovation  
  – Lean organizational structure enables rapid iteration on vehicle design, software features, and battery technology.  
  – Ability to adopt cutting-edge components (solid-state batteries, advanced driver-assist systems) faster than legacy automakers.  

• Focused Brand Positioning  
  – Opportunity to craft a distinctive brand identity (e.g., eco-luxury, urban commuter, performance) that resonates with targeted customer segments.  
  – Strong storytelling around sustainability and tech appeal can generate media buzz and early adopter interest.  

• Strategic Partnerships  
  – Potential to secure supply agreements with battery manufacturers or advanced materials suppliers on favorable terms.  
  – Collaborations with software and connectivity providers can accelerate integration of over-the-air updates and digital services.  

• Cost and Efficiency Advantages  
  – Lower fixed overhead compared to large incumbents; nimble team can optimize production processes and lean manufacturing techniques.  
  – Early use of contract manufacturing or modular platforms helps contain capital expenditures.  

Weaknesses  
• Limited Scale and Manufacturing Capacity  
  – Small production volumes can lead to higher per-unit costs, making it difficult to compete on price with mass-market EV models.  
  – Dependence on external manufacturing partners may introduce quality control challenges and supply bottlenecks.  

• Brand Recognition and Trust  
  – New entrants often struggle to build consumer confidence in safety, reliability, and service support—critical factors in vehicle purchases.  
  – After-sales network and charging support infrastructure may be underdeveloped compared to established OEMs.  

• Capital Intensity and Cash Burn  
  – Raising sufficient funds for R&D, manufacturing, and sales network expansion can dilute early investors or strain financial resources.  
  – Extended development timelines and regulatory certification requirements add to funding pressure.  

• Supply Chain Vulnerabilities  
  – Heavy reliance on a few suppliers for batteries, semiconductors, and rare earth materials exposes the startup to price volatility and geopolitical risk.  
  – Delays in component delivery can stall production ramp-up.  

Opportunities  
• Growing EV Adoption and Incentives  
  – Government subsidies, tax credits, and low-emission zones in major markets can accelerate consumer uptake.  
  – Corporate fleets and ride-hailing services increasingly seeking electric vehicles open B2B sales channels.  

• Expansion into Emerging Markets  
  – Rapidly urbanizing regions in Asia, Latin America, and Africa represent under-served EV markets with fewer entrenched competitors.  
  – Local partnerships or licensing deals can facilitate market entry.  

• New Mobility Services  
  – Roll-out of charge-as-a-service offerings, battery-swap networks, or subscription-based ownership models can differentiate the startup.  
  – Integration with smart-city infrastructure and V2G (vehicle-to-grid) platforms adds value and opens secondary revenue streams.  

• Software and Connectivity Monetization  
  – Opportunity to develop proprietary telematics, in-car entertainment, and over-the-air update ecosystems that generate recurring revenue.  
  – Partnerships with energy companies or utilities for intelligent charging management.  

Threats  
• Intense Competition from Legacy and New Players  
  – Established automakers are investing heavily in EV lineups, leveraging economies of scale and brand loyalty.  
  – Well-capitalized startups (including those backed by tech giants) pose direct threats in tech and customer experience.  

• Regulatory and Policy Shifts  
  – Changes in subsidy programs or tightening safety and emissions standards can raise compliance costs or slow market growth.  
  – Trade tensions affecting tariffs on key components (batteries, electronics) may erode cost advantages.  

• Supply-Chain Disruptions and Commodity Price Swings  
  – Volatile prices of lithium, cobalt, nickel, and semiconductor shortages can inflate production costs and delay delivery schedules.  
  – Single‐source dependencies increase risk of factory shutdowns or contract disputes.  

• Consumer Adoption Barriers  
  – Range anxiety, insufficient public charging infrastructure, and high upfront purchase prices remain persistent concerns for many buyers.  
  – Negative media reports on battery fires or recalls—even if isolated—can damage brand reputation disproportionately.

Below is example documentation for a Python class named BankAccount with three core methods—deposit, withdraw, and get_balance. After the method descriptions you’ll find a short code snippet showing how to create an account and call each method.

Class Name  
BankAccount

Class Description  
Represents a simple bank account. You can deposit money, withdraw money (as long as you have sufficient funds), and check your current balance.

Methods  

1. deposit  
   - Purpose  
     Add funds to the account.  
   - Signature  
     deposit(amount: float) -> float  
   - Parameters  
     • amount (float) – The amount of money to deposit into the account. Must be positive.  
   - Returns  
     float – The new account balance after the deposit.  
   - Raises  
     ValueError if amount is negative or zero.

2. withdraw  
   - Purpose  
     Remove funds from the account, if sufficient balance exists.  
   - Signature  
     withdraw(amount: float) -> float  
   - Parameters  
     • amount (float) – The amount of money to withdraw from the account. Must be positive and no greater than the current balance.  
   - Returns  
     float – The new account balance after the withdrawal.  
   - Raises  
     ValueError if amount is negative or zero, or if amount exceeds current balance.

3. get_balance  
   - Purpose  
     Retrieve the current balance of the account.  
   - Signature  
     get_balance() -> float  
   - Parameters  
     None  
   - Returns  
     float – The account’s current balance.

Sample Implementation of the BankAccount Class  

```python
class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, account_number: str, initial_balance: float = 0.0):
        """
        Create a new BankAccount.

        :param account_number: Unique identifier for this account.
        :type account_number: str
        :param initial_balance: Starting balance (defaults to 0.0).
        :type initial_balance: float
        """
        self.account_number = account_number
        self._balance = float(initial_balance)

    def deposit(self, amount: float) -> float:
        """
        Add funds to the account.

        :param amount: Amount to deposit; must be > 0.
        :type amount: float
        :return: New account balance.
        :rtype: float
        :raises ValueError: If amount is not positive.
        """
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Deposit amount must be positive.")
        self._balance += amount
        return self._balance

    def withdraw(self, amount: float) -> float:
        """
        Withdraw funds from the account.

        :param amount: Amount to withdraw; must be > 0 and <= current balance.
        :type amount: float
        :return: New account balance.
        :rtype: float
        :raises ValueError: If amount is not positive or exceeds balance.
        """
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Withdrawal amount must be positive.")
        if amount > self._balance:
            raise ValueError("Insufficient funds.")
        self._balance -= amount
        return self._balance

    def get_balance(self) -> float:
        """
        Get the current account balance.

        :return: Current balance.
        :rtype: float
        """
        return self._balance
```

Sample Usage  

```python
# Create an account with an initial balance of $100
acct = BankAccount(account_number="ABC123", initial_balance=100.0)

# 1) Check balance
current = acct.get_balance()
print(f"Starting balance: ${current:.2f}")   # Starting balance: $100.00

# 2) Deposit $50
new_balance = acct.deposit(50.0)
print(f"After deposit:   ${new_balance:.2f}") # After deposit:   $150.00

# 3) Withdraw $30
new_balance = acct.withdraw(30.0)
print(f"After withdrawal:${new_balance:.2f}") # After withdrawal:$120.00

# 4) Final balance check
print(f"Final balance:   ${acct.get_balance():.2f}") # Final balance:   $120.00
```

Here are three everyday customs in China that often surprise American visitors—along with a brief comparison to typical U.S. practice:

1. Tipping Is Rare  
   • China: In most restaurants, taxis, and hotels, you generally don’t leave an extra tip. Service charges (if any) are built into the bill, and a cash “thank-you” can even be politely refused.  
   • U.S.: Tipping 15–20% in restaurants and a few dollars for taxis or hotel staff is standard, and servers often rely on that income.

2. Communal Dining and Table Manners  
   • China: Meals are usually served family-style. Dishes go in the center and everyone uses their chopsticks (or communal serving chopsticks/spoon) to take portions. Slurping noodles or soup can be a sign you’re enjoying the food. It’s polite to leave a small amount of food uneaten to show you’re satisfied.  
   • U.S.: Individual plating is most common, and meals are generally eaten quietly. Leaving food on your plate can signal you’re full, and slurping is often frowned upon.

3. Gift-Giving Etiquette  
   • China: When presenting or receiving a gift, use both hands. A recipient will often initially refuse (“Oh, you shouldn’t have!”) as a show of modesty before graciously accepting. Cash gifts in red envelopes (“hóngbāo”) are common at weddings or New Year’s—white envelopes are reserved for funerals.  
   • U.S.: Gifts are often opened immediately in front of the giver, and direct “thank you”s are encouraged. Cash gifts usually come in plain cards without as many unspoken rules about envelope color.

These differences all stem from distinct cultural values—collectivism and harmony on the dining table, importance of “face” and modesty in social exchanges, and a different approach to service relationships. Embracing them can turn the initial surprises into memorable, respectful experiences.

Vegetarian Tomato-Spinach Pasta

Ingredients (serves 2–3)  
• 250 g spaghetti  
• 2 Tbsp extra-virgin olive oil  
• 3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced  
• 200 g cherry tomatoes, halved  
• 100 g fresh spinach leaves  
• 50 g grated Parmesan cheese  
• 1 tsp salt (+ extra pinch for seasoning)  
• ½ tsp freshly ground black pepper  

Cooking Steps  
1. Cook the pasta  
   – Fill the stockpot with about 4 L of water and bring to a boil.  
   – Stir in 1 tsp salt and add the spaghetti.  
   – Cook until al dente, about 9–11 minutes.  

2. Sauté the garlic  
   – While the pasta cooks, heat the frying pan over medium heat.  
   – Add 2 Tbsp olive oil and the sliced garlic.  
   – Sauté, stirring occasionally, until fragrant (about 1 minute).  

3. Add tomatoes  
   – Toss the halved cherry tomatoes into the pan.  
   – Season with a pinch of salt and ½ tsp pepper.  
   – Cook until tomatoes soften and release their juices, 3–4 minutes.  

4. Wilt the spinach  
   – Add the spinach leaves to the frying pan.  
   – Stir until just wilted, about 1–2 minutes.  
   – Remove pan from heat.  

5. Combine and serve  
   – Before draining, dip the saucepan’s rim into the stockpot and collect about 60 ml of pasta water; set the saucepan aside.  
   – Carefully pour the remaining water out of the stockpot, holding its lid slightly ajar to keep the pasta inside.  
   – Return the drained spaghetti to the stockpot, pour in the tomato-spinach mixture and the reserved pasta water.  
   – Gently toss to coat.  
   – Divide among plates and sprinkle with 50 g grated Parmesan.  

Enjoy your simple, flavorful vegetarian pasta!
